speechtext:
May I direct a question to the Minister of Labour with respect to a meeting which he and his colleagues had yesterday with the delegation of the united auto workers from Oshawa? February 9, 1967

Inquiries of the Ministry to cause dislocation in the labour force. I should like to ask the minister whether such an appeal has been made to the auto companies and, if so, what response has been received from them.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I discussed this matter with a delegation whose membership had hardly changed since November last, soon after the question also arose. I told them at that time that our approach to the companies collectively had not been too successful, and I had hoped we might work it out with the individual companies concerned rather than on an industry basis.

subtopic: MANITOBA-PROCLAMATION OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the President of the Privy Council, although I believe it should be addressed to him in his capacity as Registrar General of Canada. Could the minister tell us whether


the regulations under part X of the Bankruptcy Act, which we amended earlier this session, have been enacted; and whether part X, having to do with the orderly payment of debts, has been proclaimed for Manitoba?

speakeroldname: Hon. Guy Favreau (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Registrar General of Canada; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MANITOBA-PROCLAMATION OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my hon. friend for having given me due notice of his intention to put this question. The answer is no, but I think it requires a very short explanation.
The superintendent of bankruptcy, in cooperation with the Department of Justice, has prepared draft rules and forms for the purpose of part X, and these draft rules and forms have been sent to the provincial authorities in Manitoba for their comments. As soon as these draft rules and forms are accepted by the provincial authorities they will be submitted to the governor in council.
We have not as yet received a request from the lieutenant governor in council of the province of Manitoba pursuant to section 198 of the Bankruptcy Act that part X be proclaimed by the governor in council to be in force in that province. My understanding is that before making such a request, the provincial authorities wanted to satisfy themselves that the proposed rules and forms for part X would make the legislation operational.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 8, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Monteith.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I think my opening remark must be that in my opinion and from my experience in this house the speech made by the Minister of Finance on December 19 was the most peculiar budget speech that was ever presented to this house. I say it was peculiar because in theory the minister was saying that he advised the government to proceed cautiously in one direction, and at the same time condoned the action of the government in proceeding at full speed in the opposite direction. The minister on the one hand cautioned the government and on the other condoned the action they have taken although he is against it.
The main message I get from the budget speech is that the government is spending more money than the Canadian people can afford to spend. I think the minister has presented this problem to the house very well, although he has offered no solution whatsoever and no suggestions as to how to stop this trend. In certain parts of his speech the minister appears to advise against any action which would cause an increase in expenditures, but admits that he has been unable to convince his colleagues in the cabinet that his theory is correct, so he proceeds to explain to the nation how additional revenues can be obtained to enable the government to continue its present spending spree.
Some questions come to my mind which I would like to ask the minister. Has the minister admitted his failure to impress upon the cabinet that the danger flag is flying with

February 9, 1967	COMMONS
regard to expenditures, or are his right wing ideas being overruled perhaps by some more powerful personalities in the cabinet? Last night on television I heard a speaker say that the present government has two ministers of finance; one to tell the people what they should do and the other to advise the cabinet to do the opposite. Is the minister making provision for a way out when the balloon eventually goes up so he can say "Don't blame me. I gave you this warning but you took no notice of it"?
In my view the most important statement in the minister's budget speech of December 19-and it appears on page 11331 of Hansard -was when he said:
I want to repeat what I said in this house on September 8 and on other occasions, that we must moderate the rate of increase in new public expenditures.
Apparently the minister repeated this statement time and time again in the house but no notice has been taken by his own colleagues of what the minister said.
Further on he goes on to say:
Neither the capacity nor the willingness of Canadians to pay higher taxes should be taken for granted.
I should like to ask the minister why the government is prepared to impose higher taxes. How much money is the public of Canada paying in taxes every year? The sum is astonishing, and the minister has given us the figures in his speech. I suggest the Canadian people have a right to expect the Minister of Finance, who is supposed to understand Canada's financial position, to take steps to see that the goose that lays the golden egg is not killed.
I am afraid this is not what he has done. We have a right to expect our Minister of Finance to issue warnings not only to the public of Canada but also to the government Which is spending this money. As he said, he issued a warning to the government on September 8 and on many other occasions that it must curtail its expenditures. From all the evidence in the house it appears that the minister has voted on every occasion to accept accelerated expenditures, although he now tells the government that it should not be spending so much money.

You would get some help if you put pressure on the former minister of
The Budget-Mr. McIntosh finance. We are not quite sure which one we should support, but if the present Minister of Finance supported his own statements by appropriate action we would also support him.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Not only did the minister issue this warning; he also confirmed it in his budget speech. He said:
It is already evident, however, that our expenditures will continue to rise next year quite apart from the guaranteed income supplement.
He also said:
I now forecast that our budgetary revenues before the tax changes I shall propose would be approximately $8,240 million compared to $8,300 million forecast in the budget last March.
In fact there would be a decrease of $60 million from the budgetary revenues forecast on September 8.
The minister stated further:
Our surplus in terms of the national economic accounts I would forecast at roughly $140 million compared with the budget forecast of $455 million.
In fact the surplus in the national economic accounts will be reduced by some $315 million. The minister continued with more proof which he has apparently put before the people of Canada and before the cabinet. He went on:
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Our net financing requirements for non-budgetary transactions, before tax changes and excluding transactions in our own debt, I estimate to be $342 million compared with $190 million at the time of the budget

That shows an increase of $152 million in net financing requirements for non-budgetary transactions. These several statements of the minister add up to the fact that we are close to the point where the government is spending more than the people of Canada can afford. As the minister himself said, it is all too easy to anticipate growth in our revenues
February 9, 1967

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh and to commit ourselves to spending programs that outrun it.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is exactly what the present government is doing. Its spending is outrunning the money that is coming in. The government is even running out of ideas on how to collect additional revenues from the people of Canada. We on this side, knowing the dangers and the problem of financing the budget, ask the minister why he does not prevail upon his colleagues in the cabinet to hold the line on expenditures within the several departments. We want to know the reason that each department is not holding the line on its expenditure. I can find nothing in the budget speech of the minister to indicate that the government is making any effort to curtail its expenditures.
It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has been warned by his officials that the danger flag is flying, but that he has been unable to stop the spending spree launched by the government, or that this spending spree has been accelerated to such extent that the government has lost control of the brake and cannot stop it. It seems that each department is trying to race the other to obtain cabinet approval for the largest possible expenditure, without regard to the source of revenue.
The minister stated that to raise all the revenue which is required by all governments in Canada, which to use his figure is currently running at about $18 billion a year, a large variety of taxes and charges must be levied. This includes not only federal expenditures but provincial and municipal expenditures. In fact, Mr. Speaker, if my arithmetic is correct the tax requirements amount to $900 for each man, woman and child in Canada today. If I break that figure down, for the average family of four the breadwinner must provide $3,600 in taxes each year before he can even consider feeding and clothing his family.
This amount of $18 billion required by way of taxation every year within this nation amounts, I believe, to roughly the total amount of money on deposit in Canadian banks at the present time. In other words, almost a lifetime of savings is required to pay each year's taxes to run this country. Therefore I suggest that a halt must be called at some point. There must be a revision of our tax laws and a halt called to government expenditure until revenue catches up with expenditure.
Such a figure as that to which I have referred, Mr. Speaker, I suggest is alarming

considering the income of the average family in this country. I contend that this government should be stopped from spending more than it can afford, and stopped before we find ourselves in an accelerated inflationary period or are forced to devalue our currency to the point where it is useless as a medium of exchange. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the government must be stopped before it bankrupts the country.
One would expect, Mr. Speaker, the press and financial critics to have a responsibility to the people of Canada and to focus attention on the uncontrolled spending taking place in this country. I suggest, as others in this party have suggested, that the press are not doing their duty by failing to focus attention upon proper topics. They would much rather take something speculative or sensational and blow it up. I suggest they are not doing the service to the country that is expected of them. The press at this time should prove to the people of Canada the value of the freedom of the press in a democracy by informing them of the financial dangers which lie ahead for Canada if this government's uncontrolled spending is not curtailed.
Why is the press so reluctant, we would ask, to criticize this government and give the public the true facts? It appears that the majority of publishers are more political than the politicians, or at least more Liberal minded than the Liberals. They belittle any attempt on the part of the official opposition to offer constructive criticism at any time on practically any subject to come before parliament. The press, knowing the political affiliation of their publishers, time and time again have charged the opposition with filibustering and obstructing practically every major piece of legislation which has been debated in this house during the current session, and I would say perhaps also in former sessions.
This point, Mr. Speaker, was well documented by one of my colleagues, the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard), in a press release a short time ago, in fact directly after the debate on medicare. I should like at this time to put on record, for the sake of the press if for nobody else, this paragraph which is contained in the press release of the hon. member for Simcoe East.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does he agree?

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I agree with what he said, and it was this:
I have used this example of the needless debate on medicare because of the frequent government charges that we, in the Conservative party, are
February 9, 1967

obstructing the government's legislative program. Indeed, this charge is levelled at us every time that we are not prepared to go along meekly with whatever legislation the government brings in. We are charged with obstructionism when we opposed the Hon. Walter Gordon's first budget. That our opposition was well-founded was proved by the fact that little of that budget lasted beyond the debate stage. We were charged with obstructionism when the first Canada pension plan was introduced. But that bill, too, you will recall, was withdrawn and one almost entirely different in its concept was substituted.
I might interject here, Mr. Speaker, that to my mind either one was a monstrosity. The hon. member continued:
We are being charged with obstructionism in the bill to unify the armed forces and in our efforts to eliminate the "means test" from the present proposal to increase old age pensions only for those who have incomes of less than $60 monthly. I think I can safely claim that, in many cases where we have criticized government legislation, where we have opposed passage of the legislation in the form in which it was introduced, our opposition and our criticisms have been constructive and have been in the best interests of the Canadian people as a whole.
We make no apology, Mr. Speaker, for the action we have taken on most of these bills, or for the constructive criticism we have offered. In fact it is our duty as members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition-indeed it is the duty of all members of the opposition-to constructively criticize government legislation; and I am only sorry that other parties in the opposition have not taken the opportunity of offering similar criticism.
I wish to deal for a few moments with charges of obstruction with regard to the armed forces bill. Our criticism of the Minister of National Defence is identical with our criticism of the Minister of Finance. Both have informed the Canadian public of problems within their jurisdiction, but neither appears to offer concrete or realistic solutions to overcome these problems. This has been the basis for most of our criticsims all through this session, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Finance has told us that we are spending more money than we can afford to spend but at the same time he is making provision to spend additional sums beyond that which the government is now spending and has in its treasury. Rather than being realistic about the problems in his department and solutions to those problems, the minister has launched on a program of mystification with which he hopes to lead the public down the garden path.
23033-812J

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh [DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I am convinced that the term "unification" is coined. It means nothing. Speaking before in the house I have said that the unification issue comes down to nothing more than a change in wording, with the word "royal" being deleted from "Royal Canadian Air Force" and "Royal Canadian Navy". It may mean a common uniform for all forces but it does not mean much more than that.
For the press the unification issue was an excuse to build up a potential leader for the other side. We have been told we ought to be careful not to destroy the Minister of National Defence. Our own followers tell us, "Under no conditions do we want him destroyed. We do not want his chances to be leader of the Liberal party destroyed. So far as we are concerned, we should like to see him as leader of the Liberal party". I say, God help Canada if the minister ever becomes prime minister.
The sum total of the minister's efforts in jockeying with the term "unification" will prove, when the smoke has cleared away, that he had no conception of the real problem facing his department, the lack of any national defence policy for Canada. The problem is not whether the forces should all have the same uniform or whether the word "royal" should be deleted from the names of some formations, which the minister has shown may be done under his definition of unification. As I said before in the house, the minister's propaganda about his mysterious policy of unification will prove to be the most gigantic hoax ever perpetrated on the Canadian public. It involves nothing but a change of uniform and deletion of the word "royal".
In the process of obtaining information from the minister we in the opposition were charged with filibustering, obstruction and an anti-unity conspiracy. I tell the minister there was no conspiracy, no filibuster and no obstruction. I am sure every member who spoke on this issue was genuinely concerned about the radical change implied in the minister's press statements or in the inferences the press drew from his statements. The minister did not realize what he had implied but it became plain after the press had dealt with it that it was something very serious. In fact, so serious was this matter that a great number of senior officers in all services threw up their hands in disgust and resigned.
We do not apologize for our concern about national security. In a democracy it is not
February 9, 1967

The Budget-Mr. McIntosh enough to trust blindly that the government will decide wisely vital matters such as finance and national defence. Every responsible citizen has a duty to understand what is happening and to exercise his judgment on questions that seem complicated and difficult. It is not hard to understand that we cannot spend more money than we have. Only a certain number of sources yield money.
Even the Liberal press became concerned about the minister's lack of clarification on the issue of unification. They ventured such statements as:
One reason for the doubts and questioning of the opposition is that the government's complete plans for integration or unification are as yet vague and undefined.
Those plans are still vague and undefined. They are still mysterious. For what purpose are funds allocated to the Minister of National Defence? The situation remains the same as it has been. The government never has had complete plans in regard to national defence and it still does not have complete plans. The Liberal press has also said:
Critics of the integration program have three major objectives: 1. They want to see maintained the identity of the three services, even within an integrated defence organization.
I understand that the three services will be retained.
2.	They would like to see a halt made now in the integration program so that problems that have arisen can be examined.
There will be problems with integration but problems would arise with any process.
3.	And they would like to have a full inquiry made into future plans of the government in this field so that their impact can be properly assessed.
I suggest that on this occasion the press made a fair assessment of our objectives. The liberal press went on to state:
In the circumstances it is no more than right that the government should be willing to lay its cards on the table so that the armed services and the Canadian people can see what the government is trying to do and can then give the government's plans the consideration they deserve and should have.
After listening to the minister's introductory remarks on Bill C-243 and observing his silence with respect to questions about press statements he released, it became obvious to many of us that the government has no up to date defence policy. The minister, perhaps because he is taking advice from the wrong people, as we have suspected for some time, is not aware that in our time the technique of war is changing rapidly and that all nations

must adjust their thinking to cope with these changes. Canada is no exception. We have suggested several times that the minister look at what France has done. The French realize they have not too much money to spend. They cannot increase their national defence budget, but their armed forces are as effective, perhaps more effective, as they have ever been. The French have cut down their manpower and increased their firepower. That is what our defence policy should achieve.
For the minister to formulate a realistic defence policy he must accept some modern facts. I will enumerate some. I have said time and again in the committee and I repeat now that it is the minister's duty to inform the public of these facts rather than to bewilder them with the myth of unification. Unification means nothing; it is no different from the integration which would take place in any event.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mystification.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that is a good word. The minister has mystified everybody, including his department.
Returning to the point, first, and possibly most important, I believe the minister must accept that the only defence possible for Canada now and in the future is on a continental basis. Our friends across the border to the south have for some time developed the defence of their country on that premise. In so doing they will defend Canada whether we want them to defend Canada or not. These are facts which must be faced and dealt with. We are a proud nation, wishing to retain our sovereignty, but if we wish to share the benefits of this security we must share a proportionate burden of the cost. I do not say we should bear half the cost and the United States the other half, because we have 20 million people and the United States has over 200 million. But we should pay 10 per cent of the cost to defend the North American continent. We should be proud to pay that share in order to retain our sovereignty.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We want some say in what will take place in connection with the defence of the North American continent because, though small in numbers, we own a large part of it. In fact, the only justification for Canada having a defence force of any kind in the latter half of the twentieth century is in order to participate in some system of collective defence. This is another fact we must face. In other words, our defence policy, if any, must be based on
February 9, 1967

alliances in order to be effective. I see the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux); he will note that I say "if any". Once our forces have been dissipated in accordance with the system of collective defence to which we are committed there is not much left. So why bring in the question of unification which does not mean anything very much-a change of badges, a change of name and putting everyone into the same type of uniform?
For a number of reasons, chiefly geographical, Canada cannot afford to assume an isolationist or neutral role. The old role of neutrality has gone by the board. No country can be neutral unless an aggressor will observe that neutrality. This was clearly demonstrated during both world wars in the case of Belgium and Holland. What did it profit either of those countries to be neutral when the aggressor decided to move his forces through them anyway? This is something Canada must accept.
If the Minister of National Defence wishes now to form another force to be placed under the United Nations to act as a police force and carry out an armed police role, I would not quarrel with him. That might be a good idea if the government, in its wisdom, decided that such a thing should be done. But let us not fool the Canadian people as to the value of our forces. I say the government was right in limiting the budget of the Department of National Defence to $1.5 billion. Our role now in the collective defence of the North American continent is defined. We know what equipment we need. I suggest it should not be exceeded in the absence of good and just cause.
Before I resume my seat I should like to take this opportunity of thanking the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport for focusing attention on the government's views with regard to the Crowsnest pass rates. In a publication which I believe is issued in his constituency there is an article written by the hon. member himself. The heading is "The Crow's Nest Rates" and beneath it we read: "By James A. Byrne, Kootenay East MP". If this represents the policy of the government it is beyond me how we can ever expect to have unity within our country. I would not mind if the statements made in the article were correct. Maybe I would blush if they were correct. But they are not. Surely the parliamentary secretary, who deals with this type of thing, should understand what he is doing. I can see no
The Budget-Mr. McIntosh hope for our country when the people who are supposed to be running it for us do not understand the situation. The hon. member said in this article:
The western farm members of the House of Commons are continuing a blockade of a bill to amend the Railway Act this week-
This word "blockade" is a new one. The government has accused us of obstruction, it has accused us of conspiracy it has accused us of filibustering. But now the word is "blockade". The hon. member went on:
What is it all about? Mostly their fear, it would seem to me, that the public may be provided a means under the act to determine some of the facts about statutory grain rates, commonly known as the "Crow's Nest Rates".
Later we find these words:
The farm members, well aware that they have a good thing going for themselves (rates for the carriage of grain that were in effect in 1897) do not want the taxpayers in the rest of Canada to learn the facts.
That is an out and out lie. I think the majority of Canadians know the facts, and for no consideration would we try to hide those facts from them. In case the hon. member does not know, let me remind him of what happened at that time. There was an agreement between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian people. The hon. member said further:
Following a prolonged discussion with the government the C.P.R. entered into what hindsight has proven to be one of the most imprudent arrangements in the history of railroading.
But in any agreement there are two sides to the question. The hon. member has implied that the people of western Canada are enjoying a privilege which other people in Canada do not enjoy. I say this is an out and out lie. I could go into details about the tariff situation which we in western Canada condone.
I wonder whether the hon. member knows what the C.P.R. has obtained in return as a result of the concessions which were given under the agreement at that time? I suggest that no assessment could possibly be made now as to the advantage which this agreement brought to the C.P.R. In any case, the fact remains that an agreement was made at that time. I presume it was made by intelligent people representing the government and the railway company and both sides must have been satisfied that a good deal had been made. To say at this point that the C.P.R. came out on the short end of the stick is utter nonsense. Wise as the hon. member appears to be, and wise as he may appear to his
February 9, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Mongrain constituents, he has failed to bring out both sides of the argument. He has not only told a falsehood; he has not been fair. Let him tell us how the C.P.R. is benefiting from the agreement before he starts an argument.
Again, let him not forget for a moment what the production of wheat in western Canada means to the whole economy of this country. If he would follow this up he would find that in Vancouver, for instance, where no wheat is grown, a great many thousands of dollars flow in daily because wheat is grown on the prairies and transported to that port.
Had it not been for the revenue Canada obtained from wheat sales the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) would have been in a very difficult position a couple of years ago. It might be accepted that the Crowsnest rates constitute a type of subsidy. The fact remains, however, than an agreement was made between two bodies and once an agreement is signed that agreement sticks. We are here to see that people like the hon. member for Kootenay East and the minister he supports do not bring in by the back door something which they could not bring in by the front door.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, studying as we are in this house the supplementary budget, or rather the minibudget as it has been called, reminds us that more than ever federal budgets tend to condition our economy, to stabilize it, and to spare us the type of disastrous depressions we have known in the past.
Consideration of the consequences the budget can have leads us to examine certain deficiencies in our economy, to attempt to diagnose them objectively and to suggest remedies. For my part, one of the sorest spots, one of the most damaging deficiencies in our economy at the present time is the proliferation of labour conflicts throughout Canada.
While keeping in mind the workable possibilities of a budget on the economy, I should like to refer, as briefly as possible, to the situation regarding labour disputes, to the possible cause, in my opinion, of this proliferation of labour disputes, of strikes, if you like, to their effects on the economy and the desirable aims of those concerned with labour relations, and finally to suggest briefly some solutions which the government could consider and perhaps eventually apply through appropriate pieces of legislation.
IMr. McIntosh.!

I believe we have reached the point where the Canadian people are desperate in the face of the great number of strikes being announced every day. The point has been reached where the workers involved and the unions themselves are wondering whether strikes, as a means to settle labour disputes, are not outdated by the current economic situation and whether the time is not ripe to seek less costly solutions first for the workers but also for the public affected by the disastrous consequences of such strikes occurring too frequently these days.
To obtain a clear understanding of the situation, Mr. Speaker, we should take a look, for instance, at the number of strikes in Canada since 1961, let us say, up to 1966 inclusive. For 1966, the figures must be estimated for the last two or three months of the year. Since 1961, we have figures which are accurate enough and we find that, from 1961 to 1966 inclusive there have been in Canada, 2,870 strikes and lock-outs. This means a yearly average of 480, which represents about 40 per month. And there is no indication of any reduction in sight. Looking at the figures, they seem to be increasing every year. Some will claim that strikes are a symptom of health. I have some doubts about that.
Mr. Speaker, 2,870 strikes and lock-outs mean 11,424,050 man-days lost to the country, and I do not include the last five months of 1966, because the statistics have not yet been published. You will admit that this is fantastic. Those are days when the Canadian economy has failed to operate, when the Canadian production has brought no profit to the country. Whatever the reasons to justify that-and I submit that there are justifiable reasons-I must nevertheless say that that is disastrous to our country's economy.
If you try to assess those things in terms of dollars, Mr. Speaker, and if you take as a basis something very modest, for instance the five-day week at eight hours per day, at an average hourly rate of $1.50-everyone will agree that this is very modest and, in my opinion, even below average-this means a loss of $137,088,600 in wages in Canada between 1961 and 1966. This does not take into account the days and the wages of workers indirectly affected by the strikes, who were forced to stop working, even though they were not on strike, because certain related industries were themselves paralysed during that period; neither do we take into account the loss of income suffered by companies affected by 11,424,000 man-days lost. Mr. February 9, 1967

Speaker, I feel the situation has reached disastrous proportions for the economy of Canada.
You will note, and I wish to make this clear right away, that I am not trying to blame anyone. I want to make my comments as objectively as possible. I am not trying to find fault with the labour movement nor the government. I am trying to analyse a problem and make positive suggestions to the responsible members of government, with a view to correcting this situation because, as I said, the labour movement itself is beginning to feel this has gone too far; I am referring here to the rank and file, which does not necessarily include leaders of labour organizations who, because of their position, are not always free to express personal opinions or say everything they know; I am talking about the ordinary worker who is the first person affected by these strikes, in his personal economy.
It is therefore a truly alarming situation and, just to make the information complete, some of my hon. friends may be interested in knowing how these strikes were distributed, between 1961 and 1966. I have the doubtful satisfaction of saying that my province suffered the greatest man-day losses during this period, although this is not where the greatest number of strikes occurred. My mistake, Mr. Speaker, I am not referring to the whole period, this only covers the month of July, 1966. So that the facts may be better understood and in order to present a clearer case, I will only quote figures for the month of July 1966.
In July 1966, there were 27 strikes or lockouts in the province of Quebec, causing a loss of 445,263 man-days, whereas the 46 strikes in Ontario were responsible for 312,150 man-days lost. The other strikes were as follows: 12 in British Columbia, 3 in Newfoundland, one in Prince Edward Island, 2 in Manitoba, and 4 both in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Mr. Speaker, all this confirms what I said earlier, that the situation has become critical and must absolutely be remedied.
At this stage, I should like to quote part of an editorial published in the Montreal newspaper La Presse and written by Roger Champoux who concluded his comments on the strikes in the province of Quebec as follows:
Baffled politicians, idle civil servants, teachers flourishing signs, interns and residents in study sessions, a hundred suggestions and few solutions, 18,559 strikers in all... the sight is ridiculous. And this is only the first act.
The Budget-Mr. Mongrain
As I said, this is only the first act of the play, because there is talk of an imminent strike in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, it might be timely to question ourselves about the cause of this proliferation of strikes in our country. There are many causes, of course, and to make a cursory analysis, there is, for instance, the rising cost of living, which increased from 129.2, in 1961, to 144.2, in 1966, and which is still rising; this affects the budget of individuals who want many of the good things of life. On the other hand, workers cannot be blamed, because they need and are entitled to a minimum standard of living. According to St. Thomas Aquinas, this is an essential condition for salvation, even if it may surprise some people.
Automation, of course, is another cause, because it creates problems and causes great concern among workers. From one month to the next, some of them may be laid off and may, after many years with a firm, have to readjust to new conditions, new trades, or go back to school and sometimes leave the place where they have enjoyed their family life for many years.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Another cause might also be this sort of quest for emancipation which is going on in the world and which is not found only in Canada, but in all parts of the world. Everybody seeks freedom and wants to get rid of all restrictions, all constraints. Now, the labour movement, like all the others, has been bitten by the bug and wants to look tough to employers, and most of the time they have reasons to. This emancipation crisis has created problems, even among labour leaders who-a phenomenon more and more apparent than heretofore-can hardly control their members any more and who are often led into courses which they were reluctant to follow originally. Such a state of affairs has created some disagreements among unions, disagreements which, in my opinion, are too much in the public eye and which are not at all favourable to the progress of labour movements in our country.
Moreover, there is perhaps the obsolescence of our negotiating machinery which was suited to other times but is no longer adequate in this atomic age of ours. It must be reviewed. Our governments, it would seem, hesitate to do so because the situation grows more complex every day, the demands are piling up from day to day; the labour climate
12838	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mongrain has grown fluid and lacks the reasonable stability it had a few years ago.
Perhaps there is also the other phenomenon that is due to the restrictions imposed to control the economy and especially credit. Faced with the competition which is growing ferocious in domestic, local and world markets, some employers harden their attitude, sometimes unreasonably, which provokes the worker indirectly and leads him to resort to that extreme measure which is called a strike.
We always thought that it should only be used to deal with extreme situations. However, we wonder now if extreme situations have not become commonplace, and those who watch our economic situation, especially those who assume responsibilities, namely the members of the government, are concerned. The members of this parliament, who must co-operate with the government to ensure a sound economy, examine the results of those strikes, which are more and more numerous and find that they create problems for our foreign trade, for the delivery of goods we have sold as a result of agreements or contracts, also problems of competition on international markets. Those numerous strikes mean, in many instances, complete disaster for some sectors of our whole economy; they certainly cause a great deal of apprehension to some investors who might have been able to put back on their feet some of our wealth producing businesses.
They certainly ruin the economy of those individuals who are affected by those strikes. In fact, during weeks and months, they see their debts piling up at the grocer's and other stores because they are not getting any pay. And what about all the family problems this implies. Those strikes constitute, in many cases, especially when they are related to public services, a sort of penalty on the public in general, which is to the prejudice of the common good and in many cases, involves extremely serious consequencies that I cannot discuss at length right now for lack of time but that might perhaps be usefully analysed most carefully one of these days.
And all those numerous strikes contribute in the end to the worsening of this climate of emancipation I was referring to a while ago, this climate of revolt, to use a word that might be more accurate and will express more exactly the situation, this climate of revolt that is certainly unhealthy, that often

DEBATES	February 9, 1967
finds expression in open and organized rebellion, in fields where, up to now, everyone admitedly respected what was called authority, which should still be termed thus and without which we will drift into anarchy before long, confusion before long, and the first to be affected will be precisely those workers we are attempting to protect.
Mr. Speaker, after analysing all these things, it might be advisable to set forth some principles. We might ask ourselves what our objectives should be before considering remedies to rectify this alarming situation; what should be the principles motivating the labour leaders, the government, the members of parliament and all those who seek remedies to these problems?
There is one principle mentioned here, in the C.L.C. report which was published yesterday following an interview with the government. It mentions the measures to be taken to settle the labour situation:
It should be something allowing the settlement of disputes in fairness and objectivity.
Fairness and objectivity, it will be understood, obviously require that we consider everybody's welfare, first, that of the workers concerned, who are entitled, like everybody else, to a reasonable share of worldly goods, but also, let us not forget it, the general welfare which we are agreed to call the common good.
Mr. Speaker, I have found elsewhere a description of what should be the main objective of those who are concerned with finding solutions to the numerous labour disputes. This is an article which was written by Mr. A. H. Raskin, assistant editor of the editorial page of the New York Times. This article was published in June 1966, in the magazine Atlantic Monthly, and was reprinted in the November issue of the Labour Gazette-and I shall open a parenthesis here to point out to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) -

So that he will be aware of the situation, I point out to the minister that the French edition of the Labour Gazette which has just been issued is the edition for the month of November. It is at least two months late.
Therefore, as Mr. Raskin was saying:

For the community, the most important question is whether collective bargaining can be used to protect the interests of the general public, and not only those of the unions or the management-
February 9, 1967	COMMONS
That, again, was Mr. Raskin, and the quotation is taken from an article of his published in the Atlantic Monthly. He asks the question and, a little further on, suggests several solutions himself, to which I shall come back later. Meanwhile, I should also like to mention something which the labour congress said yesterday should be the aim of all those concerned with the settlement of these disputes, and I quote from an article published in La Presse yesterday:
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The C.L.C. recognizes that the government is responsible for protecting public interest, sustaining the economy and fulfilling Canadian commitments abroad.
Now, that is just fine; it is comforting to know that labour itself understands these major objectives. Naturally, it raises certain objections further on; for instance, and I quote:
We are absolutely convinced that the government will not solve labour problems by limiting or refusing workers the right to withdraw their services, by forcing them to return to work against their will.
Here we must ask ourselves: do workers seek the right to strike for the fun of going on strike, or are they seeking it to solve their problems? To my mind, the answer is obvious: workers do not want the right to strike for the fun of going on strike: they want to solve their problems.
Therefore, if we could find another formula, if a more modem technique could be found to settle labour disputes, I am convinced that the workers themselves would be the first to applaud and rejoice, since they would no longer have to suffer the hardships of strikes.
The C.L.C. report adds:
This is usual practice among dictatorial governments throughout the world, but it surely could not be applied here.
That would be dramatizing the situation a little; it would be true if we were really trying to abolish strikes, without any substitute acceptable to all parties concerned.
Our main objective therefore, Mr. Speaker, must be the common good. That makes it simple and clear-cut. What then, would the remedies be?
I do not want to be so presumptuous as to try and invent them all by myself, Mr. Speaker; for that matter, I readily admit that my ability in this field is quite limited. However, the Economic Council of Canada recently made public certain suggestions which were discussed in an article published
The Budget-Mr. Mongrain in the January 31, 1967 issue of Le Devoir. Among others, there was the following statement:
The measures suggested by the council in order to ensure adjustment of manpower to technological changes deal with giving notice of changes to workers, natural cut-down in personnel, elaboration of transfer programs, transferable pension privileges, and the creation of labour-management committees in every factory governed by a collective agreement.
This is an important suggestion:	"the
creation of labour-management committees in every factory governed by a collective agreement".
Labour-management committees would function the year round with the help of neutral advisers from outside the factory.
This last comment is my own. Now, to continue:
The document published by the Economic Council also suggests three financial measures which collective agreements should also take into account; these would become applicable when recourse to other means would not compensate for all losses of employment due to technological changes.
These are: a generous lay-off allowance, supplementary unemployment benefits provided by a fund to which employers would contribute, and mobility allowances.
Naturally, the economic council refers here to workers affected by automation or by drastic technological progress. But there are surely other reasons for strikes, other problems must and could be settled as one-I will come back to these later-by implementing in a general formula the creation of labour-management committees operating all the year round, with the help of expert and impartial advisers.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, I am not the only one to think that the time has come to do something. I said so in this house a few weeks ago.
Mr. Walter Reuther, a respected leader of an American union said, following the New York transportation strike, which took place I believe in January 1966, and I quote from memory: It is time for the governments to devise some machinery which would prevent the workers, when they belong to a labour union and when they have a problem to settle, a problem affecting utilities, from always having recourse to costly strikes. It is time to find up to date machinery. That was Mr. Reuther's testimony and I think that I am very objective. Earlier I quoted the evidence given by the C.L.C. and we could discuss it much more fully, but I would not
February 9, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Mongrain want to labour the point. I see for instance that the CL.C. suggested as a remedy:
Among those measures, the C.L.C. advocates a critical appraisal of the level of government expenditures in the field of construction, the abolition of the existing sales tax of 11 per cent on building materials, the need to extend immediately welfare programs and the need to ease our tight money policy.
And this is the objective:
The purpose of those policies should be to promote good and steady development of our economy.
I take this excerpt again from a summary of the C.L.C. brief published yesterday in La Presse. But it seems to me, after reading the brief presented by the C.L.C., that it suggests negative rather than constructive formulas and that it settles some aspects of the problem but not the overall problem.
I think that the most efficient remedies- and here again we could quote another excerpt where remedies are suggested-might be centred around some headings.
For instance, the federal government must undoubtedly continue and increase its control of the Canadian economy to prevent it from going suddenly through a period of recession when the worker has to tighten his belt to the point that eventually he becomes impatient to have recourse to claims which are not always objective.
Then, the federal government must try and control the economy in order to guarantee, inasmuch as is reasonably possible, to all the sons of the nation, that minimum standard of living to which he is entitled. That is beyond argument and in this connection I think it must be said that the government has already done something. On the other hand, perhaps it should still accentuate its policy and direct it mainly towards the protection of the small defenceless people, of the workers, rather than toward the protection of certain financial powers which can take care of themselves.
I was impressed, for instance, when I heard the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), during the debate on the National Transportation Act, say that this bill is greatly concerned with the protection of financial interests of the railways but very little with the protection of the financial interests of workers.
I think that the hon. member for York South hit the mark there. But the government should also be urged to modernize considerably its labour legislation in view of

the new problems facing the labour movement.
Once again, time will not allow me to give all the details. I am sure that the minister himself receives lots of briefs and that his own experience suggests to him many measures which could be included in an up to date labour code. In my opinion, it is urgent to go ahead with it.
I will now deal, Mr. Speaker, with what is probably the most important of my suggestions-which I mentioned earlier-namely that we should find a way to generalize here, in this country, those permanent bargaining bodies made up of representatives from labour and management which would include experts, economists, neutral people who are not on the payroll of employees or employers and who will take part in the discussions to express their views. I would not even be against government negotiators who could, if need be, point out the principles which determine the common good.
Such bodies should operate all year round- not only after the conflict had been going on for months and months-to try to prevent labour conflicts as much as possible.
It might be advisable for the federal Minister of Labour, of course, to hold regular meetings with the provincial departments of labour to synchronize the efforts of all the provinces and the federal government. But this is something which the minister is well aware of, I am sure.
I further suggest, Mr. Speaker, that provision should be made for the creation of labour courts as soon as possible. We should not have to look around for special negotiators, special mediators, and other interminable investigations every time disputes arise.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I believe we should have permanent labour courts in Canada. I know that workers will fear that the members of these courts would simply favour the employer; I also am aware of the fact that employers will fear that these same people might favour the employees, but I submit that mediators must be chosen in our midst or else we will get nowhere. When a dispute arises, we refer the whole matter to ordinary courts of law; but if labour courts were established, presided by the most competent personalities, people who are cognizant of all aspects of the labour problem, there would be no need for strikes, in most cases, because the parties involved would accept the verdict handed down by these labour courts.
