speechtext: I have only a sentence to say and I will not abuse this privilege, Mr. Speaker. I thank the house for its kindness and I will merely summarize my remarks. According to Canadian public opinion, the proliferation of strikes has reached an alarming degree and I think that all governments concerned, whether federal or provincial, must give urgent consideration as a priority to introducing and enforcing, without delay, after consultation with the parties concerned, the legislation suitable to the needs of 1967.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first congratulate the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) on the excellent, dispassionate, clear-headed and objective speech he has just made. He has touched a raw nerve in our body politic and he has done it, I think, in a most objective way. There is no doubt that last year demonstrated a wastage of millions of man-hours and effort at a time when this world can ill afford it. I think it is tragic, when society is now reaching with the calm assurance of success to probe into outer space and the planets which we once thought were forever beyond our reach, that we should still be struggling with an archaic and obsolete system of dealing with our major problems. I suggest that the genius of mankind which has brought the world to where it is today, if one defines genius as being a capacity to take infinite pains, should surely bring us to a position where we cannot afford to allow this situation to continue. I hope the government will examine and heed the words which the hon. member uttered.
At this stage in the discussion of a budget it is sometimes difficult for an opposition member to say something new, particularly with regard to this budget. Hon. members who were overseas during the last war will recall posters hanging in the railway stations and bus depots in the United Kingdom with a giant finger pointing to the passengers and
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin bearing the caption, "Is this journey really necessary?" I would think this is the sort of poster which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) should have had in front of him but with the word "journey" blotted out and "budget" put in its place, because it takes a certain amount of shrewd ingenuity to discover why this budget was necessary.
My colleagues in this party and other opposition members have demolished with such clarity the features of the budget that there is not too much to say about it. I think one could call it the Muhammad Ali budget. Like the unfortunate victim of the so-called sporting event the other night, the budget has been knocked down so often that it is now wilting and drooping and does not present much of a target to anyone else who wants to take a poke at it. I think it will probably sink into the oblivion of parliamentary history as the budget which was unwept, unhonoured and unsung. In fact, it never should have emerged from oblivion. However, it does give us the opportunity, as an opposition party, to cast before the members of the government those pearls of wisdom which the opposition is presenting with increasing efficiency and effectiveness, but unfortunately with no tangible results indicating that the government is taking heed of them to any extent.
I should like to deal with two matters which I hope are of interest to the house and possibly to some limited extent to the country. I want to comment first on what I consider to be the failure of the government to follow through with the program of northern development which the previous government undertook with such a marked degree of success and such a measure of accomplishment. The minister who is responsible for this department has made some gestures in this respect. I am afraid, however, that he seems to lack the full support of his colleague in this very essential part of the development of our country at the present time.
I have made one or two suggestions in the past with respect to this question. On one occasion I dealt with what I thought was the necessity of a greater degree of international co-operation in scientific improvement and techniques with regard to northern development. I was very interested, when looking through an editorial in the Christian Science Monitor of yesterday, to see that my views as to this objective are shared by this independent newspaper. I will not quote the editorial in full but it points out that Scandinavia, Canada, the United States through the state
February 9, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin of Alaska, and the U.S.S.R. have complete control of all areas of the north and of the Arctic. The editorial suggested some steps which might be taken because of this particular fact. It suggested that great advantages could be reaped from the nations concurrently seeking to develop these lands. It was suggested that this could perhaps be done through a Northern Area Institute in which geologists, physicists, meteorologists, agriculturists, and many other natural scientists from America, Canada, Russia and the Scandinavian countries could pool their discoveries and help correct each other's mistakes.
It seems to me that relations between the east and the west are not fraught with such serious difficulties as they were. There is not the same measure of hostility now, and I can think of nothing more useful at this stage in the development of our resources, bearing in mind the necessity of providing for a vastly increasing world population, than making arrangements for the proper settlement of the north. I do not mean the kind of settlement we have now wherein all too often people and corporations go into the north with one idea, to explore, exploit, lay waste and retire. We want people to settle, live, and make their homes in the north. It seems to me that the research which might be pursued independently to a limited extent by the scientific apparatus and people of these nations might, if pooled, bring about a greater degree of improvement, a greater realization of our joint hopes to settle, live in and harvest the rich resources of northern Canada and the northern parts of these other nations.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
There is another matter about which I wish to speak. The time has now come when we should have some clarification of the very confused situation and the doubt and uncertainty which prevail in regard to confederation, our constitution and what is to be done, what changes are needed and how we will obtain them. I was not in the house yesterday but I read the dialogue between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) and the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). Unfortunately, the minister did not intervene actively in the debate but acted more as an irritant at the time. Mind you this is a very essential part of our parliamentary system. We might have an opportunity to hear from the minister later on this very serious and developing situation. The matter has come more to the fore recently 
because of the exchange of correspondence between the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the premier of Ontario following the announcement in the speech from the throne at the recent opening of the Ontario legislature in connection with the holding of a constitutional conference. I have the correspondence here. I think it would be interesting to read into the record parts of what was said by the premier of Ontario and also the reply of the Prime Minister of Canada because I think that the correspondence, together with the answers of the Prime Minister given on orders of the day and at other times in the house, indicates the point of view and the attitude of this government. The last paragraph of the letter of the Prime Minister to Mr. Robarts is important and I believe should be considered by hon. members. After being somewhat critical, in the usual polite way in which these documents are formulated, of the fact that the government of Ontario was taking the initiative in this matter the Prime Minister went on to say:
It seems to me that an alternative to the approach you have suggested could be developed that would be consistent with the practice hitherto. The initiative that the government of Ontario has taken in raising the subject could, if you so wished, be translated into action through having an item suggested for possible inclusion on the agenda of a federal-provincial conference that might be called in the normal way at some time in the coming months. While no conference is scheduled at present, there is no reason why we could not explore-
This is a word beloved by statesmen, who use it frequently in their correspondence.
-with provincial governments the desirability of having a conference and determining when this would best suit the convenience of all concerned. Alternatively, you might, of course, think it best to use the vehicle of an interprovincial conference as a first step.
I would say that this was in effect a complete brush-off of the proposal made by Mr. Robarts.
Mr. Robarts replied in a letter dated February 1, 1967, which contains some views of which this house should take heed. He said in part:
Then there was need for unity. Today there is a swelling chorus of millions of voices expressing a similar need. Perhaps once again, in some measure at least, by appropriate discussion in a conference, unfettered by the techniques and procedures in effect at the various types of conference held over the past several years, achievements might result from representatives of the governments of Canada sitting down together: to examine confederation and to take stock of the state of affairs after one hundred years of partnership together: to take the time to discuss and review, in an atmosphere
February 9, 1967

free from rancour, areas of agreement and disagreement; and to explore through our ingenuity and kinship what can be done to ensure a strong and united Canada.
Surely no harm can result from conducting an inventory of the happenings and events of our century of progressive history since 1867. Out of it, in my opinion, can come suggestions for plans to chart our future and to shape the second century of our nation Uased upon a sure and firm foundation.
The penultimate paragraph reads as follows:
The one objective I have in mind for this conference is that it will serve the interests of the Canadian people and their nation which the provinces created and in whose continued existence, unity and strength, the provinces are vitally concerned.
I say amen, as should all other members, to this very statesmanlike and sensible suggestion.
Following the announcement by the government of Ontario in its speech from the throne some questions were asked in this house. For example, I observe that on February 1 the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) asked the Prime Minister whether in view of the statement made by the premier of Ontario the premier of Quebec would also be interested in taking part this year in a conference on the constitution. The question was as follows:
Would the Prime Minister agree to change his attitude and take right now the initiative in calling such a national conference?
The Prime Minister answered:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should wait for the prime minister of Ontario to reply to my communication before making further statements on this.
Some questions were asked by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and the answers which were received indicated quite plainly that the Prime Minister did not think very highly of the suggestion eminating from the province of Ontario and did not intend to do anything about it.
I think this is the only impression that can be obtained by anyone making a fair, objective and rational examination of the documents and of Hansard. The impression I get is that the Canadian government is not really interested in this subject at this time, does not want to think about it, does not want to talk about it, and does not want to give any information, mainly because it does not have too much to give, but also does not want anybody else to do or say anything about it. Surely the reason for this is not that the matter has not been brought to the attention of this or previous governments or to the

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin attention of provincial governments, and surely it must be acknowledged that there is a very urgent need at this time for a review of the situation and an attempt to make the rules conform in a better way to the present requirements.
In 1964 I placed a resolution on the order paper in which I suggested the following:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should forthwith consult with the provinces for the purpose of establishing a centennial constitutional conference to consist of a given number of Senators and members of parliament and an equal number of members of all of the provincial legislatures: which conference should meet in Ottawa and in all of the provinces to consider amending the British North America Act in accordance with the experiences of the past, the exigencies of the present and the needs of the future-
However, the fortunes of the draw were not with me and I never had the chance to have the resolution debated. Other hon. members have brought up this question from time to time, and so have members of the provincial legislatures, learned professors and people interested in and concerned about the needs of Canada. They have said: we cannot ignore any longer the necessity of examining the present-day situation, the status of the constitution and the relations between the federal and provincial governments, and so we must see what if anything can and should be done about it.
It seems to me that what in effect the Prime Minister is saying is: "Do not worry about it. We are going to look at it. We have some experts and we have my parliamentary secretary who is advising these experts. Some day this body will labour and produce something to show for its discussions." The impression I get from listening to what the Prime Minister and other ministers have stated both in and out of the house is that the whole subject is something so rare, so precious and so exclusively in the domain of experts that ordinary common mortals must not be allowed to give their opinions or help in any way to mould and shape the form which our constitution must take during the course of the next 100 years.
I think that perhaps the Prime Minister visualizes a scene some day in the future when like Moses he will ascend the mountain and some time later will come down, clutching to his bosom stone tablets on which will be engraved new changes to the constitution. He will then say in a tone of wonderment and joy: "Look what my experts have hatched up. This is not to be questioned. The experts have produced it." At that point all that the people
February 9, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin will be able to do will be to fall down, worship and say: "Hosanna, wonderful, great, we will accept it."

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that not what you would expect the conference to do?

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
By no means, Mr. Speaker. I would like to see a conference held in every province in this country. Such a conference should have been started several years ago. I do not expect it to come up with changes in a final, finished and polished form, but surely the people who are the beneficiaries and who will be affected by the changes made to the constitution should have some say before and not after the event. The minister knows-I think he is a practical man-what happens. When the experts are finished with the matter it will come before a parliamentary committee, though not with any intention of changing it. It will then be presented to the nation as a fait accompli.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I should like to see a number of these conferences held at which people will have an opportunity to express their views and opinions. There should be a great national debate carried on in all parts of the country. Perhaps the debate is one which will never really be concluded, but when we can say at a point in time that we have reached a certain stage, certainly the matter can then be handed back to the experts to polish, finish, and put the proposals into practical legislative terms.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Is this not the equivalent of what is taking place in Quebec now with les Etats generaux, the general kind of debate where all of the intermediary and pressure groups will be represented to give their opinions? Or would it not be what I have been told it would be, a meeting of premiers, leaders of oppositions, heads of national institutions, etc? .

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would hesitate to suggest to any province the form which its own inquiry should take. I think that is a matter for each province to determine, having in mind what changes are to be made. It should also be borne in mind that the people of Quebec, the people of Alberta, the people of British Columbia, the people of all the provinces, are also Canadians and must be affected deeply and fundamentally by the problems now confronting us, such as the fact that there is not a clear and decisive line of demarcation in certain areas as to problems which various


governments must solve. I think that each province should establish its own forum of inquiry. I will not suggest what is desirable for the province of Quebec, but my view is that it is essential at this time that this step be taken so that before the experts are finished the voice of the people will have been heard and felt.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But is there not such a debate going on in Canada at this time? How many conferences, seminars, lectures, panels, has the hon. member been invited to in the last two or three years? How many conferences and royal commissions have we had on the future of confederation, on this and on that aspect of our constitution? I would simply suggest that the debate is going on now. If the kind of conference the hon. member has in mind is one only to examine and analyse what is taking place and to suggest answers, then I dare say we have already had it.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What we have had is a series of hole-in-the-corner discussions. There have been a very few open and legitimate discussions but not of the type that I envisage at which each provincial government must take the responsibility for canvassing, in the way it thinks best, and securing a body of opinion from its citizens or its citizens' representatives. In recent months we have seen examples of the problems posed because of the present obscurity of certain constitutional lines of authority, problems involving manpower, education, security, pension plans, medicare and transportation, and so on. All of these problems intimately affect and concern the lives, fortunes and futures of the people of Canada.
All I want to achieve is some means by which these people can indicate whether they want their provincial government or their federal government to deal with questions of medical health, certain questions of transportation, certain questions of pensions and pension rights. During the course of such discussion debate of a far more tangible and meaningful form will take place. When this debate has concluded and the matter crystallizes-this operation should have been commenced years ago and been in the process of conclusion today-then the experts will put into final form the proposals which will be made.
Let us remember once and for all, Mr. Speaker, that all too often this business resolves itself into a matter of two dogs quarrelling over a bone: the civil service and
February 9, 1967

establishment in the provinces struggling with the civil service and establishment of the federal government, each one anxious and desirous to retain the spheres of authority they now have and to enlarge them. I do not say that this is done deliberately, intending to do harm, but that is the nature of an establishment of this kind; it is reluctant to give up any form of authority.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, governments and legislatures as well as parliament have failed in their attempt to solve the problem. What I am suggesting is that in his own way the prime minister of Ontario has indicated that he feels some attention should be paid to providing a means of securing an indication of the views of the people of his own province. I suggest this proposal should be adopted by all provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit another question? Would the premier of Ontario need federal authorization to set up such a seminar or conference within the borders of Ontario?

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did the minister ask whether he has the right to do this?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can see no constitutional, legal or practical impediment. I suggest that he not only has the right to do it but has a duty to do it at this time. I would say that every premier has a duty to undertake a responsibility of this kind. In fact, they are two or three years too late. The initiative should have been taken by the federal government. Ottawa, Mr. Speaker, is very remote from Peace River and from other parts of this country. What happens here sometimes reaches us in a very diluted form. For the people of this country to be seized of knowledge of this problem, steps must be initiated to bring it home to them through a debate of the kind I have mentioned.
As I have pointed out, there are a great many fields of jurisdiction where there is room for doubt. I can think of some examples where the best interests of the people of Canada would be served by deciding to give to the provinces certain jurisdictions which they do not now possess. Equally, I can think of a number of areas where the best interests of the people of Canada would be served by investing in the federal government certain rights which it has exercised but not always legally. There are some rights that I submit
The Budget-Mr. Forest we should make certain are legally exercised by the federal government.
There was some mention of federal-provincial conferences. They have a useful purpose but I think this purpose has been exaggerated. These are conferences where the experts burrow into the darkest corners and holes of secrecy and privacy. Sometimes this is essential, but the difficulty is that I am afraid this sort of thing is emerging in the form of a third form of government, a type of government where there is not the same degree of publicity or the same measure of criticism, argument and examination. True enough, Mr. Speaker, it may be said that all of the proposals which are discussed and canvassed and which ultimately emerge in the form of legislation are brought back to the respective legislatures and to parliament. But once they have become crystallized in a certain form and are brought forward as legislation, governments being what they are there is very rarely any hope of changing them. While they have a function to serve I caution the government to be most careful about trying to build federal-provincial conferences into an ad hoc third form of government which the people of this country have never given authority to the provinces or federal government to exercise. It may be nice and tidy and easy for the governments to do this but it is not, I repeat, in the best interests of the Canadian people.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I believe that premier of Ontario has served a useful purpose with his proposal. I hope it will be copied in various forms in other parts of Canada. Before the debate is through I hope that the minister, who has been most helpful, may see fit to present the government's views on this issue.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the supplementary estimates tabled last December by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) have been well received, generally speaking, in spite of the limited increase in personal income tax and the increase in the sales tax levied against manufacturers to finance the pension supplement granted to our senior citizens; it might not have been as well received by those who think that social measures are thus becoming less popular because they have to be paid for immediately through new taxes.
The Minister of Finance proved to be a practical man when he made it clear to the people that the government could not increase
February 9, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Forest social benefits without getting the money somewhere.
If all social benefit increases were introduced in this way, that is by offering a gift with the right hand and presenting the bill with the left, everybody would then be in a position to determine whether, at a given time, any additional levy imposed on the taxpayers and on the country's economy would constitute an excessive burden.
During the last few years, government expenditures in Canada, at all levels, have increased considerably and if we do not curb or stop them, they might bring about a reduction of investments in Canada and make our competitive position more difficult on the international market.
It is a fact that more than 30 per cent of our gross national product in Canada is absorbed by taxation and such a situation is not only frightening but unfavourable to our country, because it brings not only our economic development to a standstill but it lessens initiative, dampens any liking for risk and prevents the achievement of many plans.
Government expenditures in Canada increased from $12,098 million in 1961 to $16,127 million in 1965, that is an increase of 30 per cent in five years, while in the United States, during the same period, they increased by 25 per cent only, in spite of larger expenditures due to the war in southeast Asia.
If we figure the percentage on the basis of population, per capita, and if we consider that the population in Canada has increased much more than in the United States, our increase then is 24 per cent and that of the United States only 18 per cent. The Canadian people must be concerned, and rightly so, about that serious situation which could be detrimental to our economy and our standard of living.
One way to reduce taxation is to increase productivity and the labour output. The federal government has given these goals priority, in an attempt to improve present possibilities, and to give everyone the education and training which are indispensable in this day and age.
We will improve our competitive power by developing more highly qualified professional management and skilled labour.
The state of our economy and its future must become a growing concern because, compared with it, all other matters lose importance. Our people would not accept a

lower standard of living without creating upheavals.
Our economic experts have warned us that 750,000 new jobs must be created by 1970, and this need must induce us to modify certain obsolete economic concepts, to consider new methods.
The normal growth of our population will require industrial expansion, but automation and improved production methods will reduce the number of new jobs thus created. New needs will have to be created; we will also have to encourage industrial research in order to discover new products, different materials or improved finished products, so as to get the markets and open up new avenues.
The greatest discovery of the nineteenth century is said to have been that of the creative approach. More and more, creativity is the prerogative of organized research, particularly in the manufacturing industry. Technical progress depends more and more on organized research for innovation and improvement.
Economists generally agree today that investing in education and research is just as important as capital expenditure. Progress is not so much a function of the amount of money invested in machinery and factories as of technical improvement which can be expected from a given investment.
The supremacy of the United States on world markets is mostly due to innovations, new ideas in industry and ability to invent a great many new products; all this in turn depends on performance in research development.
Industrial development requires an extensive activity promoted by governments in industrial research.
The announcement made in the past few days by the Quebec government concerning the establishment of an important international research centre in electric energy should therefore be particularly welcomed.
Mr. Speaker, we should become less dependent on the United States for capital and new industries by urging our fellow-citizens in various ways to invest their money, their savings, in our Canadian corporations, especially those which develop our natural resources. We should put our own means to a more efficient and a more productive use.
We must consider what we could do in order to strengthen our position without unfairly penalizing foreigners who have invested here
February 9, 1967

their money and their competence tor their own benefit, of course, but also for ours.
We must take positive action in order to secure a more efficient control over our economy and to reduce our trade balance deficit.
Several methods have been suggested to make our economy sounder, better adjusted to our needs, to our aspirations and among those, the establishment of the Canadian Development Board can, under certain conditions, make it possible to channel the savings of Canadians toward the promotion and the development of our industries and resources.
However, it would not be an adequate replacement to an effective policy designed to promote private investments to merely provide enough protection and some relief in taxation.
An improved legislation designed to protect investments and the purchase of bonds and shares of our corporations is essential, especially in the light of some recent events.
Canadian and foreign companies should also be required to supply complete and more detailed information on their financial structure. Succession duties should be abolished or substantially altered. Some provinces have already indicated their intention to alter them. In my view, in an area where both the federal and provincial governments collect taxes, there should be agreement reached on that score.
These succession duties produce very little, slightly more than 1 per cent of the federal government revenue, but on the other hand, they are a major drain on capital available for investment.
We all know that some families had to sell their business or their private industry to strangers in order to avoid this tax or else they have taken up residence elsewhere to avoid these high duties. There is also the fact that several families, several people from Europe or elsewhere, might be interested in investing their capital in Canada if such duties were abolished. We are faced with the progressive disappearance of capital built up in this country and which should serve the economic progress of the country.
The Carter commission, which was established in 1962, is scheduled to present an early report. It will doubtless suggest a thorough shake-up of the entire tax structure and a more sensible distribution of the taxation fields.
The Budget-Mr. Crouse
In the meantime, the government must maintain its policy of promoting production, exports, a more advanced technology and investment of our own resources in our economy.
Canada will not succeed overnight in financing its own development and in eliminating its present trade deficit with other countries, but it should right now continue to revise its economic policy to achieve long-range objectives, which are possible if the effort is made.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

subtopic: ADDITIONAL FINANCIAL MEASURES OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the mini-budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) on December 19. Speaking as a Conservative I commend the minister for his frank review of our economic situation. His statement was a strong reminder to all Canadians that additional welfare measures must be paid for out of their own pockets.
However, in view of the size of the surplus in the old age security fund, a surplus in excess of $350 million at the end of last October, I think the minister placed undue emphasis on this aspect of expenditure. In fact, the hon. gentleman when introducing his budget seemed to be looking for a scapegoat on which to lay the blame for his government's deficit. He pointed his finger directly at the senior citizens of this country and blamed them entirely for the tax increases which seemed to be necessary. However, his statement served only to emphasize the smallness of the pittance we are giving to our senior citizens even when there is a means test attached to it, a test which would have to be taken every year in which a supplement was paid. We in the Conservative party believe that our senior citizens should have been given this increase as a matter of right without the necessity for a means test. We do not think an attempt should be made to lay the blame for the government's deficit on senior citizens who through no fault of their own need a little assistance in their old age.
What did the Minister of Finance do? In the present government the right hand does not seem to know what the left hand is doing. The minister tells the economy to go forward and backward at the same time. He raises the general sales tax, making it 12 per cent instead of 11 per cent, a move which will bring about an increase of approximately 2 per cent in prices at the retail level. What effect does this have upon Canadians?
12848	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Crouse
A large contractor in the plumbing and heating business in my constituency has written to me bringing two points most specifically to my attention. He states:
1.	To date there is no way to escape paying the increase on materials, ordered, but not delivered, before December 31, 1966. This also applies to contracts entered into months ago. In our business this is going to amount to a sizeable amount of money. The suppliers will not absorb the increase nor is there any provision in our contracts under which we could collect it from the owner. So, unless a change is made, we are stuck with it.
2. Of course insult was added to injury by exempting certain materials. We inquired about a list of exemptions and we were told that those materials exempt before June 14, 1963, will remain subject to the 11 per cent tax rate-big deal. Naturally, there must be some reason for all this but I am sure that only the Liberals could dream it up.
This serves to increase the price of homes, for example. What is needed at the present time are measures which will increase the tempo of housing construction in Canada. The price of houses and factories should be reduced, not raised. The increase in the sales tax hits not only the millionaire but the average man with a family who is already finding it difficult to pay his bills in Canada's inflated economy, as well as the old age pensioners whom the budget was designed to help.
Some of our senior citizens are today subsidizing their basic old age pensions. I refer to the minister's action in declining to retire the bonds issued by the Liberal government in 1936. I raised this matter in the house on previous occasions when I deplored the action taken by the government in this connection. As a result of my concern over this question I have received a letter from a lady in Ontario. It reads as follows:
The bonds of any responsible government are not normally bought for speculation. Most purchasers regard them as a vehicle to earn a modest rate of interest in the meantime, and provide a retirement nest egg that can be liquidated as older age needs arise. Certainly we can recall the speculation in the bonds of some weak European governments following the first world war; but I can recall no case of British, Canadian or U.S. purchasers of their government's bonds over the last 50 years having received the lack of consideration or integrity given those citizens who entrusted their savings to the Canadian government in 1936 in exchange for perpetuals regarded as safe as the old time British Consuls.
As it has turned out, the "oldsters" who needed the money have been obliged to sell at losses of 20 per cent to 40 per cent or more to speculators, but to what extent who can say? But the fact that some have been sold reflects either dire need on the part of the owners, or complete loss of confidence in the integrity of your government.

DEBATES	February 9, 1967
No responsible company doing business in this country would permit their bonds to sink to such values, if only to protect their own good name and credit rating. Some companies even support their common stock by buying it in when the price falls excessively, assuming they have funds available.
Can it be that the Canadian government is on the verge of bankruptcy, and unable to refund a relatively modest issue? If so, God help your reputation both at home and abroad.
This is a copy of a letter which was sent to the Minister of Finance. It is indicative of the feeling of Canadians about the manner in which the government is dealing with the country's finances. With this type of thinking on the treasury benches, I can only describe the Minister of Finance as a wrong-way Robin Hood who robs from the poor in order to give to the poor while extracting for Mitch and his merry men a token to be paid the hunters whose job it is to make certain that the aged and needy have no other income.
The minister has stated that approximately $18 billion is required annually by all governments in Canada, and I deplore the shameful manner in which he has singled out our senior citizens as the target or the excuse for his recent tax raises while ignoring many other government expenditures which deserve to be questioned. There is no evidence that he and his colleagues plan to attack this problem at the core, namely, the waste and extravagance practised by the government which have brought about a sky-rocketing, inflationary spiral of prices in Canada.
Surely the taxpayers who are now required to surrender even more of their savings to provide for the cost of a guaranteed income plan for pensioners have a right to expect some evidence of increased efficiency in government and some restraint in government spending. But what are the facts? The record of the government's financial position, according to the minister, shows that this year's expenditures will reach a record high of $8,580 million, and since corporate profits are lower than the minister anticipated his revenues have dropped and Canadians are still not paying their way despite all the taxes which are being levied upon them.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I ask the minister what has happened to the theory of cyclical budgeting? In times of economic boom we were supposed to have a surplus budget so that in times of economic depression the government could prime the pump with deficit financing. What do we see today? We are told by the Minister of Finance that Canadians never had it so good,
February 9, 1967	COMMONS
that In fact the economy is so overheated the minister must apply the brakes. But if we are enjoying an economic boom, why are we having budget deficits? The minister cannot have it both ways.
The fact is that Canadians are dancing but they cannot pay the piper to the tune of approximately $340 million in this fiscal year. What does the minister promise us for next year? More of the same. Listen to his words as recorded at page 11331 of Hansard for December 19, 1966:
It Is already evident, however, that our expenditures will continue to rise next year quit apart from the guaranteed income supplement.
As a smokescreeen the minister then listed as his reasons the commitments in equalization payments to the provinces and substantially increased assistance for higher education. He knows that if we criticized these reasons it would be like criticizing motherhood. We are not going to fall into this kind of trap, but some of the government's policies and programs are open to criticism.
I say to the government and to the minister that if they believe they have the right to control the economy of Canada through the imposition of new taxes, which in effect limit the spending of Canadian citizens, then it is up to the government to examine its own position and set an example of good housekeeping. Any argument that this cannot be done, that savings cannot be made in administration, is indicative that the barnacles of indecision and the rust of indifference have settled deeper and thicker on the Liberal hull than has been realized by many Canadians.
There is a growing concern among many of our citizens that they are being swept up in a whirlpool of bureaucratic controls from which there is no escape. The list of payroll deductions grows longer and longer, and with prices inflated by excessive taxation the average Canadian the man earning $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000, is having extreme difficulty making ends meet. In my opinion the government must take action on this pressing problem. Failure to do so could have serious effects upon the Canadian economy within the next 18 months.
The minister may well ask, where do we begin? The Auditor General has stated that government overhead has increased by 20 per cent in the past three years, and a study of the report of the public accounts committee should give the minister some leads in the right direction. For example, they recommend
The Budget-Mr. Crouse an end to payment of C.B.C. production employees for work not performed. At present union agreements put employees on the job even when there is no work for them to do. By eliminating this wage bill when current union agreements come up for renewal the government owned corporation could save $450,000 annually.
In my opinion public funds should not be disbursed for work not performed, and the government should direct the C.B.C. management to halt this practice. Incidentally, when is the government going to appoint a president for this organization? Today the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that question, and I listened carefully for the answer. We were told that the C.B.C. has a president, but it is my understanding that the president, Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, has tendered his resignation. Whether or not this resignation has been accepted is open to question, but I believe that a crown corporation should be managed just as efficiently and as independently as one run for profit.
Nobody doubts that Gordon MacGregor runs Air Canada, but when I look at some of the C.B.C. programs I begin to suspect that the C.B.C. is somewhat like a rudderless ship operating without a captain. I cannot help but believe that this is exactly what is wanted by the so-called creative minds employed by the corporation. The idea is to keep things in an uproar. They believe in the freedom of the C.B.C., freedom being an all-embracing word which should cover their bad taste, sensationalism and irresponsible actions. In Nova Scotian language, this is nothing but bilgewa-ter.
However, if this is the way these so-called artists want it and if there is no one in authority to direct them to do otherwise, then Canadians can call themselves lucky that the creative talents of the C.B.C. clique have not produced programs even lower in entertainment rating. Quite frankly, I believe in responsible freedom for the C.B.C. but not in the right of its hired staff to air anything they individually regard as reputation making or reputation breaking, without any interference. They may make great personal reputations by resorting to sensation-mongering, but this is not the purpose for which the C.B.C. was established.
The Canadian people are subsidizing the C.B.C. by more than $100 million a year. I say that in the public interest it is time for parliamentary intervention in the operations of
12850	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Crouse this sacred cow. The government has the responsibility to find a programming boss for this organization, and the sooner this is done the quicker the government will effect savings on C.B.C. operations which have gotten entirely out of hand.
Another field in which I believe the government could pare expenses is its foreign embassies and missions. I know these are necessary, but a periodic audit by our external affairs department would indicate to the people serving in our embassies throughout the world the truth of the finance minister's statement that neither the country nor the willingness of Canadians to pay higher taxes should be taken for granted.
Defence planning is very much in the news these days but the spotlight should not be thrown entirely on the problems of unification. More than a shudder went up and down the spines of many people when they heard the Auditor General report that more than $7 million went down the drain for bomb toss computers we did not plan to use, and that inadequate planning for low level radar installations led to extra costs of $3.5 million.
However, without question the most extravagant waste of taxpayers' money has been through the establishment by the Liberal government of the commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. In three and a half years the government has set up 15 commissions, but this has been the biggest and most bewildering of all commissions. To date it has splurged more than $7 million, with no visible, concrete results for anyone. Its purpose, as I understand it, is to alter the shape and style of our country. But in effect it has only served to rub salt in the wounds of division between our two founding races. In my opinion it has created greater disunity in Canada than any other act by a Canadian government since confederation.
A wound will never heal if it is ripped open every day, and I ask the government to terminate the hearings of the B. and B. commission and let it bring in a report. I ask this not only on behalf of the Canadian taxpayers but also in the best interests of Canada as a nation. It should now be evident that it is impossible to pass laws demanding that a man be bilingual or bicultural. This commission was set in 1963 and its members have been drawing salary and expense cheques of $120 every sitting day. Every Canadian is aware of the French and the English fact. I 
DEBATES	February 9, 1967
believe that if we could do away with hyphenated Canadianism we would build a better Canada.
These are some of the changes which could be made by the Minister of Finance if he really desired to bring expenses in line with government income. If the minister does not act to help bring this about, it is possible that Canada could face another exchange crisis in 1968. It is not inevitable, but all the elements of a crisis are now in existence. It originated with wage increases far in excess of productivity increases last summer and fall, and it is sustained by a continuing clamour for parity with wages in the United States. It is also strengthened by monetary and fiscal policies which will continue in the foreseeable future to inhibit the capital investment in productivity needed to overtake these wage increases. Quite frankly, in my opinion the Canadian economy is being priced out of competition.
If this process continues exports will fall, imports will increase and the deficit in current account will widen to the point where Canada can no longer pay its way in international transactions. In the meantime the awareness of these developments is a large factor in discouraging foreign investment in Canada, while encouraging Canadian investment abroad.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The government is obviously aware of this situation as indicated by the advertisements put out by the Department of Trade and Commerce which urge Canadian businessmen to export. This is supported also by the fact that the department has set up an export advisory council. Personally I hope these efforts are successful. I believe the minister is sincere in trying to do a good job. As I say, I hope these efforts are successful because among this country's principal needs are more investment funds and managerial talent. In some instances the one follows the other.
There is, however, a biblical quotation which states that one cannot serve two masters, and from experience we know that a house divided against itself cannot stand. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) cannot be given a voice in the government. This is a man who proposes further bureaucratic measures such as the Canada Development Corporation, a man whose budgets had to be completely withdrawn because they almost brought about the downfall of the Liberal government when he was finance
February 9, 1967	COMMONS
minister, a man who opposes foreign investment capital. You cannot give such a man a voice in the government and expect the investment community, both Canadian and foreign, to show confidence in this government and in this country.
Those who wish to lead must give some evidence of their ability along these lines. However, as long as maritime Gordon, as he is affectionately know in Nova Scotia because he wanted to give its people a one-way ticket to some other part of Canada, remains in the cabinet it will be difficult to establish confidence in the minds of Canadian and foreign investors that Canada offers better opportunities for their investment funds than other areas of the world. To clear the air with regard to these differences within the cabinet, the Prime Minister should make an early statement of policy on foreign investment in this country.
Having suggested to the minister a number of proposals which if implemented would effect some savings, I should like to turn to the Atlantic provinces, an area of Canada still haunted by excessive unemployment and one which could use some of the funds presently being wasted in the departments I have mentioned. My own province of Nova Scotia has gained recognition internationally for its stable institutions, its intelligent and adaptable labour force, and its strategic location in the trading world. However, though we can rightly feel encouraged by this progress we can hardly feel satisfied. We have not as yet narrowed the gap between average incomes in Nova Scotia and those in central and western Canada. The simple fact is that we are still too dependent upon forms of employment which do not offer good prospects for growth. We must continue to modernize our economy because despite the progress which has been made unemployment still is twice as high in the Atlantic provinces as it is in the rest of Canada.
To help narrow the gap I believe the government must put forward more programs which will help us progress at a faster rate. This is necessary because we are so far behind; we seem to have to run like the devil just to stand still. Our concern is also increased by the changes we see developing under this government which could be harmful to our Atlantic economy. For example, no longer do we have regional allocations for ship repair work. We are concerned about the effect any changes in our army, navy and air
The Budget-Mr. Crouse force bases will have on the Atlantic provinces. We are watching with interest as each year the government builds at tremendous cost larger icebreakers to keep the St. Lawrence river open for shipping, because this cannot but have a very adverse effect on the ports of Halifax and Saint John. Surely there must be some quid pro quo to offset the damage to our economy which these federal policies are bringing about.
There is much to be done. For example, there is the causeway to Prince Edward Island which must be finished. There is a corridor road to be built through Maine which would bring Montreal within a five-hour run of the maritime border. Such a road would literally bridge the gap separating the mari-times from the markets of central Canada. Then there is tidal power to be developed in Minas Basin. The last of these projects would provide the cheap electricity we need to entice secondary industry into Nova Scotia and the maritimes. Once it was established the sale of electrical energy would amortize its cost over the years.
The Minister of Finance should also take some steps to help our tourist industry. Last year, for example, the United States government brought forward the date for free entry of antiques into the United States from the year 1830 to 1860. The free entry date for antiques coming into Canada is 1847. The tourist industry is of great importance to our country, especially Nova Scotia. Under the existing laws controlling the entry of antiques, Canadian dealers cannot compete with United States dealers when buying abroad. Dealers in the United States can import duty free goods manufactured at a later date than the goods we are allowed to import. This increases our costs considerably. Many United States citizens come to Nova Scotia to buy antiques and this is a stimulant to the country's economy. Since we are celebrating our centennial in 1967 I suggest to the Minister of Finance that one of the steps he might take by way of celebration would be to permit free entry into Canada of antiques manufactured in 1867 or prior thereto.
One of the steps which the Minister of Finance could take immediately would be to declare the entire Atlantic provinces a designated area so that it would be eligible for benefits under that program. This would attract industry to the Atlantic provinces which is now forced to go to other areas of Canada. This is especially true if such industries are

There are few countries where there is a greater need than in Canada for specific regional policies and for additional instruments which are capable of being applied on a differentiated basis from area to area.

Followed with energy, reasonable foresight, and consistency, in a favourable climate of public understanding, these approaches should be capable of progressively diminishing the problem.
I commend these thoughts to the Minister of Finance and to the government. I hope they will follow the sage advice of the economic council so that the people of the Atlantic provinces and of Nova Scotia in particular will share equally with other Canadians in the economic benefits of a developing nation. Why, then, the imposition of tax increases related to the old age security fund and the 1 per cent increase in the sales tax? This was the minister's method of saying thank you to our senior citizens for their past contributions to the growth and development of our country. He is saying, in effect, that if taxpaying Canadians want to see the senior citizens of our country decently housed, and have adequate food and clothing and a few extra dollars for medical and social needs, then the taxpaying Canadians must pay for it. There is no reason why senior citizens should not share the fruits of present increases in view of their past services and contributions to our economy.
The increase of 1 per cent in the sales tax was uncalled for. The exemptions on building materials and food were necessary, but the housewife was hit in other areas such as family needs for clothing, appliances and furniture. This tax, imposed with apologies, will doubtless increase the prices of the items on which it is imposed because the retailer and manufacturer will merely pass it on to the consumer.
In exempting housing materials from the 1 per cent increase in sales tax the minister recognized the serious housing problem facing Canada today because of both housing shortages and the high cost of houses. On November 21 last year the Ottawa Citizen indicated in an editorial that I was exaggerating when I stated in the House of Commons that Canada is facing the worst housing shortage in its history. However, when the facts are reviewed the results are more in line with my conclusion. In 1966 construction starts on new houses amounted to 134,474 units compared with 166,565 units in 1965, a decline of almost 20 per cent. What is the picture for 1967? The Economic Council of Canada in its third annual report set a goal of 170,000 dwellings a year to take care of the increase in population and new family formations.
Mr. Hignett, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, stated in the Globe and Mail of Tuesday, January 31, 1967, that he was doubtful about starts going much above 150,000 this year. It is obvious we will be falling short of the projected goal of 170,000 this year, which does not take into account replacement of older houses. The 1961 census showed that of a total of 4,500,000 single dwelling houses 2,500,000 were built before 1945, that nearly 25 per cent of these houses do not have bath or shower facilities and that 21 per cent are without flush toilets.
Mr. David B. Kirhup, an economist and statistician for the Toronto Real Estate Board, made an interesting projection of housing needs in the future. He stated that it took Canada 100 years for is population to reach 20 million but it will only take 35 more years for the number to reach 50 million. This means that from 10 million to 12 million new housing units will have to be built by the year 2,000, an average of 300,000 to 350,000 dwellings per year. He also stated that one-third of all Canadians live in only eight major cities. If the present trend to urbanization continues five cities, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, will house 35 per cent of all Canadians by the year 2,000. A lot of new accommodation will be needed in the cities. This projection is indicative of the serious attitude toward housing that must be taken by all levels of government.
Many Canadians have asked why there is a housing shortage. We in the New Democratic Party feel that there are at least five major reasons for the shortage. First, all levels of government are blind or apatheric to the housing crisis. Federal, provincial and municipal levels of government are failing to take their full share of responsibility to solve the housing problems; second, the moneys available for housing have been diverted into
The Budget-Mr. Gilbert the building of shopping centres, office buildings and high rental apartments because of the high rates of interest payable in this sector; third, the high rates of interest payable by the purchasers of the new homes, now range from 7J per cent on N.H.A. loans to 8 to 8J per cent on loans from conventional lenders such as insurance and trust companies; fourth, the high cost of building materials and the high cost of serviced land in urban areas and, fifth, the failure of C.M.H.C. to promote its aims and purposes.
I should like to develop these five reasons a little further and then suggest a program of action that should be seriously considered by the government. I have said that all levels of government have been blind or apathetic to housing problems in Canada. The federal government has failed to take the initiative in setting up a federal ministry of urban affairs and housing which would be responsible for the co-ordination of the national housing needs of the country, with the necessary consultation with the provinces and municipalities. It has taken the position of the friendly banker and has regarded housing on the basis of an economic tap to be turned off or on depending on economic conditions in the country at the particular time. The provincial and municipal governments have not taken the initiative in determining housing needs, more especially in public housing and housing for senior citizens, and have not co-ordinated their physical housing needs with federal financial assistance to meet these needs.
I quote the following from the Toronto Star of Friday, January 20:
The apathy of municipal governments has deprived the poor of public housing in Canada, the Senate-Commons prices committee was told yesterday.

In an editorial in the Toronto Daily Star of Monday, January 16, 1967, this argument was set forth. The editorial reads in part:
This is one of those projects which sounds wonderful when you say it rapidly, but which looks increasingly impractical when you examine it in the light of present day realities.
Let us consider, for example, the position of a tenant earning $5,000 a year-one of the group this proposal is apparently intended to benefit.
At the present time, it is virtually impossible to build or purchase a new three bedroom house in Metro (except perhaps in the most remote suburbs) for less than $20,000.
If the corporation charged only 5 per cent interest on the purchase price-and this is far below the going rate and would require subsidization-the interest payments would amount to $1,000 a year.
Let us add to this $250 a year for taxes and $300 for heat and utilities. Our $5,000 a year man is now paying $1,550 annually or 31 per cent of his income.
This is equivalent (in terms of per cent of income) to the highest rent the O.H.C. charges. It goes beyond what is considered a reasonable percentage of family income for housing.
Yet in all these calculations, we have so far made no provision for repayment of the principal owing -in this case $20,000.
It is obvious that if realistic monthly or quarterly principal payments are added to the interest in the usual manner, the burden would be altogether too great for a man with a $5,000 or even $6,000 income.
The only way O.H.C. could sell houses on this basis would be by not only subsidizing the interest rate but by forgetting about repayment of the principal-in effect making the purchaser a present of the capital value of the house.
This would be an inordinately expensive procedure. To supply a relatively few people with homes of their own, the corporation would have to cut back drastically on its funds for building or buying rental accommodation for those in need.
Moreover, the houses it sold would be subtracted from the stock available for public housing, and might easily wind up being sold to some real estate speculator-perhaps to become the nucleus for a new slum.
The establishment of the Ontario Housing Corporation represents public recognition of the fact that the province has an obligation to help provide decent living accommodation for those who cannot provide it for themselves. But it is wholly unrealistic to try to extend this into an obligation to provide full ownership of a house for everybody.
Having made its bow to the spirit of Toronto past, the O.H.C. should quietly bury the whole idea.

The subject matter of this motion concerns a matter which in my view represents a piece of uncompleted legislation in the sense that a very important part of an act that has been passed has so far not been acted upon by the government. While there may be times when I would readily agree that the kind of documents asked for in this motion could be properly considered as privileged and it might not be in the public interest to table them in the house nevertheless I feel that under the particular set of circumstances prevailing in this case the general rule has in effect ceased to apply. I believe the time has come when we in this house and those Canadian citizens who are particularly interested in this question should have some factual knowledge of what has been going on rather than being left, as we have been over such an extended period, in a sort of never-never-land on this particular matter.
I hope to be able to prove my point, Mr. Speaker, largely by means of words which have come from the mouth of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) on this subject. In order to do that I should like to recall to the memories of the minister and other hon. members something of what he had to say about the act referred to in the motion when the bill was brought before the house for second reading on May 20, 1964. My motion has to do with the co-ordinates involved in the determination of base lines. On

[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
The second important purpose of the bill is to apply the straight base line system to the Canadian coast line. This part of it, unlike the section concerning fishing zones, will be of an enabling character. When the bill comes into effect the Governor in Council will be authorized to draw straight base lines. The question may be asked: what does this achieve? In response, I would say that what the bill accomplishes is of great significance. It makes applicable the straight base line system to the Canadian coast. These straight base lines will be drawn in accordance with international law, on the basis of the decision of the International Court of Justice in the Anglo-Norwegian fisheries case and of the Geneva convention on the territorial sea and fishing zones and taking into account Canadian historic interests in the bodies of water off our coasts.
Then he went on to say:
... it makes applicable, on proclamation, the general system of straight base lines to the Canadian coast line. The authority that is given to the Governor in Council is with respect to the specific lines to be drawn and the exceptions to be made. The larger effect of the bill is to make applicable the principle of the straight base line system to Canada. Hon. members will note that the bill specifically provides that all areas enclosed by the new straight base lines will be internal waters of Canada. This is important and may have far reaching consequences.
He also said:
I am convinced that in taking this action now- as the government is doing, unilaterally-Canada is acting in accordance with present day international law and practice. The government is convinced that we are following the wisest course in immediately seeking agreements with the countries affected by our action.
Later he referred to the pros and cons of the course Canada should have followed after having referred certain things to a Geneva conference on the law of the sea. He said:

Canada had to make a choice. There were two possibilities. We could have decided in favour of postponement. This would have meant an indefinite delay. This would have meant that we would not have for a long time the 12-mile fishing zone which this legislation will make possible. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up much of the time of the house, since apparently there was an agreement that we might rise before seven o'clock for the supper hour. However I want to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) for giving us the opportunity to have a brief debate on this important subject.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the law of the sea w th regard to the width of national fishing zones and national waters has been a very live issue for a number of years, joined with the tendency to make greater and greater demands on the living resources of the sea as a source of food, especially by countries such as Japan, which have a relatively small agricultural base and big populations.
It will be recalled that at one point the United Nations convened a conference in Geneva to try to reach agreement on the width of territorial waters and straight base lines. There were two conferences. The Canadian proposal, which was known as the Six Plus Six formula, provided for territorial waters with a width of six miles, plus an exclusive fishing zone of an additional six miles. That proposal failed to carry by a very small margin.
Th's was a great disappointment to Canadians, and in the next election campaign there was much loose language used by certain people with respect to this item. I am not
Motions for Papers
looking at the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) when I say this, but representatives of his party did indulge in this loose talk. They said, "Why, there is no problem at all. All that is lacking is resolve on the part of the government of the day. If we should come to power we will wave a magic wand, the foreign fishing vessels will disappear over the horizon, and there will be no more problems. All we have to do is unilaterally declare a 12-mile zone, and everything within a straight base line is Canadian waters for the exclusive use of Canadian fishermen."
However, when the Liberal government came to power it found the problem was not qu te so simple. My greatest objection to the course being followed by the government is on the long delay in coming to a conclusion; but an even greater misdemeanour, if one may use that term, was perpetrated by the Liberal party in leading the Canadian people to believe that this was a simple problem that could be quickly and satisfactorily solved.
From experience I know there are great difficulties involved, but the question in the mind of the fishing industry is, where do we stand now? I recognize the necessity for a period of negotiations during which the negotiators on behalf of the Canadian people would not disclose the exact situation, while still in the midst of the bargaining process. But it should be recalled that the government was about a year in office when it had this legislation passed, and the legislation itself did not declare unilaterally that the straight base lines system would be brought into effect.
The bill had the effect of creating exclusive fishing zones from the nearest coastline, ex-clud ng nations that did not have historic fishing rights; but the important thing dealt with by the bill was the establishment of headland to headland base lines which would enclose large, important bodies of water, such as the gulf of St. Lawrence, the bay of Fundy and Hecate strait. The catch, however, was that the base lines were to be established by order in council following negotiations with foreign countries. These negotiations have now been going on for three years.
Only history can tell which is the better of two possible approaches to a problem. When I was minister of fisheries my colleagues and I felt that negotiations should be advanced as far as possible before one started to wave a big stick, saying what one would do unilaterally. In some respects our bargaining position may not be as strong as we would like it

Technically I agree with the government that these are privileged documents which should not be produced, because if they were produced it would create a bad precedent. Nevertheless the government in conscience cannot go on year after year telling us the negotiations are continuing, and that it is doing everything it is possible to do. This may be perfectly true; but we have to accept the government's word for it, and no matter how sincere its judgment may be it is bound to be a judgment which favours its own position. The time has come when parliament and the Canadian people must be let into the government's confidence, unless of course that would destroy the hope of an imminent agreement being reached.
But if real progress is not being made, then the government may have to take the responsibility of starting all over again, and possibly of taking action to initiate another law of the sea conference. If such a conference were held now I believe fhe Canadian proposal might carry, because in the interim there has been much change. There are many new members in the United Nations, and in addition many countries which attended the previous conference have since unilaterally declared 12-mile exclusive fishing zones.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the two hon. gentlemen who have just spoken, that this is a matter of considerable importance to the fishermen of our country. Strictly speaking, the motion which is before the house is not one which would allow us to examine the government's policy with regard to establishing a 12-mile fishing zone based on the straight base line principle. However, I understand the interest of the two hon. gentlemen and other members of this house in the substance of the proposition, and therefore I have not raised a point of order.
The issue before the house is not whether the government has made progress in its negotiations. The issue is whether the house should be given documents which have been exchanged between the government of Canada and other governments. That is the issue before the house, and nothing else. I would submit

and indeed the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) has agreed that this is the case-that it is not right for hon. members to ask the government to disclose the house the contents of documents, aide-memoires, and letters which have been exchanged between one government and another in respect of negotiations which have not yet been completed.
It is clear why parliament has devised this rule, because if the rule were otherwise it would not be possible for the government to carry out its diplomatic intercourse and it would not be possible for the government to maintain its diplomatic position in its negotiations with other countries. It is clear that until such time as negotiations have been completed, those negotiations would stand in jeopardy and would suffer if there should be a premature disclosure. I do understand however the impatience of hon. gentlemen. I share that impatience, and so does the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) who has toiled arduously during the past two and a half years in an effort to implement the full provisions of the bill.
The situation briefly is this: We passed a bill authorizing the establishment of the 12-mile fishing zone that is now in effect. It now is the law of the land. There was objection to this measure. Indeed, it will be recalled that when the Prime Minister met with President Kennedy at Hyannis Port in the spring of 1963, the Prime Minister intimated that it was the intention of Canada to establish a 12-mile fishing zone and that we proposed to do so by measuring the 12 miles not on the basis of the
February 9, 1967

sinuosities of the coast but on the straight base line system. The president was not too happy about this declaration of intention. The government nevertheless, while recognizing the cordial relations which exist between our two countries, caused such a measure to be introduced into the house.
As I have said, the law of the land provides that there be a 12-mile fishing zone. This was done because of the frustrations which were experienced by others who had sought to achieve the same thing by the process of international conference. I am not criticizing the former government for having tried by the conference method to bring about what we did legislatively. My friend, the hon. member for Queens, has discussed this matter in most objective terms tonight, and on the other occasions when he has participated in this debate. We felt however that the conference method, desirable as it is and preferable as it is, had not succeeded in achieving its purpose. There was then no other course open to us but to resort to a legislative measure in order to do what other countries-almost half the countries of the world-had done by unilateral action.
So, we have before us an accomplished fact. We could not establish the straight base line system without at the same time asserting with success ownership of certain bodies of water over which we claim a proprietary interest and title. The negotiations with the United States and other countries such as Spain, France, Norway and others have been protracted. They have taken a longer time than I ever anticipated they would. But no one can criticize the government because of the action taken by other countries with regard to our proposal to establish the initial measurement of the 12-mile system based on the straight base line principle.
All has not been in vain. Not only have we established a 12-mile fishing zone, but so also has the United States. As a result of the action taken in this house we have built up a jurisprudence in this matter. There can be no doubt that the United States would not have embarked upon the establishment of its 12-mile fishing zone, in the light of the attitude it took at international conferences when an effort was made to resolve this question, if it had not been for the fact that our parliament at the instance of this government did establish the 12-mile fishing zone.
It had been my hope that we would have been able to start to establish the co-ordinates long before this. As my friend, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni observed, I did say
Motions for Papers
that perhaps by the beginning of 1965 we might be able to do so. But we had to make a choice between doing that and subjecting ourselves to litigation, which would have caused a greater delay than these negotiations have caused or, I am sure, will prove to have caused.
I believe it will not be long now before we will begin to establish some straight base lines. I do not say that we will complete them, but I believe we will be able to establish some straight base lines very soon. If we do not I will be greatly disappointed. I am making this prediction on the basis of my assessment of the state of the negotiations now with a particular country. I am awaiting a reply to a proposal that the government made as a result of negotiations between the Minister of Fisheries and myself with the United States. I believe that we should hear from the United States within the course of the next few days. When this reply reaches us we will have a better appreciation of when we can begin to establish co-ordinates and straight base lines, and when we may take other steps to further the objective we have in mind.

I believe that, while the negotiations have taken a year and a half longer than I thought they would, the fact is that during that time we have steadily built up a body of opinion to the effect that the Norwegian case is not without application to Canada in the situation we are discussing.
On the question of procedure, it must be clear that I cannot agree to tabling the documents sought in this motion. Hon. members know that diplomatic usage does not permit the government to make available to the public without the consent of the other party, the instruments used in negotiations, until and as long as agreement has not been reached. Whether or not we have this consent from the United States I feel we would not be discharging our responsibilities as a government if we agreed, on our own, to such disclosures. This would make difficult any further negotiations we have with other countries.
This question has been decided many times in the house. My hon. friend, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), it will be recalled, on October 6, 1963, moved for a copy of cabinet minutes and other official documents authorizing the Secretary of State for External Affairs to notify the executive director of the International North Pacific Fisheries Commission
