that the commission's recommendation for removal of halibut stocks in the Bering Sea had been accepted. I pointed out on that occasion that it was a well established rule in Canadian parliamentary practice that documents and cabinet minutes could not be revealed, for the very reasons I am advancing in this instance. Our procedures clearly establish that documents involving international negotiations which are still incomplete cannot be made available against the wishes of the government, and certainly not without the consent of the other government and without the consent of the other parties to the negotiations.
I remind my hon. friend of a decision in this house on January 24, 1955 when the then secretary of state for external affairs, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), refused to produce an exchange of letters between the government of Canada and the government of the United States concerning the imposition by the United States of total or partial impediments to the importation to the United States of some agricultural products. The then secretary of state for external affairs said that this motion concerned diplomatic corresondence with a foreign government and dealt with negotiations then in progress. He said that according to well established practice of the house, this information was privileged and it would not be possible to table it. That motion was withdrawn.
Likewise in 1957 a motion was made by an hon. member for the tabling of the preliminary report concerning hydroelectric development of the Columbia river system in Canada. The then acting minister of northern affairs and national resources, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) expressed his opposition. These reasons undoubtedly were in the mind of the hon. member for Prince, who concurred in the position I am taking with regard to the application of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I am sorry, I meant the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean). The hon. member is such a prince I always confuse his status with that of his colleague's constituency.
This is what the hon. member for Calgary North said on that occasion:
-negotiations with the United States In regard to the Columbia river system and the development of hydroelectric power on that system have been going on and will probably continue for some time. We do not consider it in the public interest that this document should be made public during the time these negotiations are in progress-

That motion was actually voted on and was rejected.
There have been a whole series of other similar requests. My hon. friend, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud), played a part in a similar request for documents under similar circumstances. That request was rejected on June 5, 1963. The minister refused the production of a copy of a recommendation of the International North Pacific Fisheries Commission, and all exchanges between the government and the commission and other parties relating to this recommendation. As a result of his opposition the motion was modified.
On May 5, 1965, the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), found himself in the position of refusing a demand for documents concerning an agreement between the governments of the United States and Canada providing for free exchange in the automobile industry.
We are all familiar with these precedents which one could go on reciting. I think the case for the request is so clearly contrary to our practice and procedure that I am not asking too much of the hon. gentleman, now that he has delivered himself of his irritations and impatience, to acquiesce in the request to withdraw the motion which, in the interest of what he seeks, should not be adopted. I ask my hon. friend not to lose heart, because I am sure he will find that the negotiations the Minister of Fisheries and myself have had are not inconsistent with his objective, and very much in the interest of the fishing industry and fishermen in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, just prior to the six o'clock adjournment I had set forth the fourth reason why we in the New Democratic Party think there is a serious housing shortage in Canada today, and I said that it was due to the hight cost of building materials and the high cost of serviced land in urban areas. I put forth the builders' claim that the cost of home building had been cut to a minimum, and I quoted from an article in the Globe and Mail which supported the builders' contention.
Another aspect of this matter is the high cost of serviced land in urban areas, which is a very serious problem. This has been caused by land speculators. May I note that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) who is in charge of housing, has been urging Canadian cities to become active in the land market to prevent the prices of lots being forced upwards by speculators. He indicated also that federal legislation has existed since 1949, empowering the C.M.H.C. to help finance residential land development, but he indicated that the provinces and municipalities are not making full use of it. The minister said:
It is our view that provincial and local governments in Canada by a large scale commitment in this activity could market serviced lots at reduced prices at no net cost to the taxpayer either federal, provincial or local.
I agree with these views. However, encouragement should also be given to these bodies to change the expropriation laws in the provinces to ensure that fair and reasonable compensation is paid for such expropriated lands.
The fifth reason is the failure of the C.M.H.C. to promote the aims and purposes of the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act. The housing programs financed by N.H.A. and C.M.H.C. have not begun to take care of low income persons. For example, in 1965 the average income of a borrower under N.H.A. was $7,200 and in 1966 it was $6,600. No help was provided for persons below the $6,000 level. In fact, figures indicate that only 8.5 per cent of N.H.A. loans were given to persons earning between $4,000 and $6,000 and .5 per cent to persons earning under $4,000. This reminds me of Professor Murray's saying that this is socialism for the rich but not for the poor.
Another important aspect is the high percentage of income that a person must pay toward principal, interest and taxes. The

The Budget-Mr. Gilbert gross debt service of these three items is not supposed to exceed 27 per cent of gross income according to N.H.A. regulations. This amount is too high. The striking feature in this pattern is that those families which can least afford it spend proportionately more for their housing, and usually get the least value for their money. For families earning less than $4,000 and purchasing homes under the N.H.A. in 1965 the average ratio of gross debt service to income was 29 per cent. For families earning between $4,000 and $6,000 it was 25 per cent and for those earning $10,000 or more it was 13.8 per cent.
The rule of thumb commonly used is that shelter costs should not exceed 20 per cent of income, rising possibly to 25 per cent if such services are included as heat, light and water in rental accommodation, or principal, interest and taxes for home ownership. Such a ratio must be adjusted for persons in the low income brackets to take account of their family needs for a decent and adequate standard of living. For example it has been suggested that a family with a net income of $200 per month should not spend more than 15 per cent on shelter costs.
The federal government has failed to take the lead with the provinces and municipalities to ensure that homes are provided for persons with low incomes and for senior citizens.
Having attempted to set forth reasons for the failure by ail levels of the government to find solutions to our housing problems, I should like to suggest the following 10 point program to meet the problems:
1.	The setting up of a federal ministry of urban affairs and housing, with the C.M.H.C. being directly responsible to the new minister and having the responsibility of suggesting an overall housing policy for Canada based on surveys of housing needs conducted by and in consultation and co-operation with the provincial and municipal authorities.

2.	The federal government through C.M.H.C. should make available large amounts of money for new houses, public housing, senior citizens housing and co-operative housing. The target for the next three years should be at least 250,000 new homes a year to take care of increases in population, new family formations and replacement of older housing.
3.	Moneys for the new projects should be obtained by the sale of home bonds guaranteed by the government in denominations of

$500 and $1,000, repayable in five or ten year terms and bearing interest at attractive rates for sale to Canadian people and firms. Canadians who bought war bonds during wartime to protect Canada will be prepared to buy home bonds in peacetime to build Canada.
4.	Rates on all new mortgages to purchasers of homes should not exceed 5 per cent, and the federal government should subsidize interest rates above these levels either by income tax adjustments or by direct payments. All mortgage loans should include, if necessary, an extra $2,000 for the purchase of fixtures, furniture, furnishings and appliances.
5.	There should be large-scale land assembly projects initiated by both provincial and municipal levels of government, with financial participation by C.M.H.C. This would cut down the high cost of serviced land in urban areas.
6.	Assembled lands by provincial and federal governments should be leased for development purposes, enabling reduced prices of serviced lots and community control over land use.
7.	Municipal services relating to urban renewal schemes such as schools, recreation centres, parks, streets and sewer improvements should be included in the total cost of an urban renewal project and subject to the three level cost sharing. The cost of renewal should include the relocation and renewal expenses of displaced residents and business firms. Displaced homeowners should be offered special loans to help purchase a replacement property, if they cannot obtain suitable housing with a moratorium on repayment of the special loan until the property is sold.
8.	Direct loans below market interest rates should be provided to low income families for property improvement.
9.	Senior citizen homes and public housing must be an integral part and a first priority of any crash housing program.
10.	We must study and develop new techniques for the mass production of housing and the streamlining of building codes. Habitat is an excellent example of new building techniques.
If the government were to adopt the above measures and develop them into a housing program for Canada, Mr. Speaker, we would be facing our next hundred years with a sense of purpose, pride and concern for all

Canadians. Our pledge should be: Decent housing for all Canadians as a basic right guaranteed by government action.

In view of the fact that the money is there, that these people have paid it in, and that many of them have retired, five, 10 or 15 years ago, some of them on a pension of $50 a month, I think that this should be reviewed right away. The money belongs to these people and I think that this should be re-assessed.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on a matter which is often spoken about in

the house but which perhaps requires action rather than words. I should like to speak of education and educational expenses, although in a purely constitutional sense as it affects this house, instead of wasting my time on dreams which do not take into consideration the present constitutional realities in Canada.
The proposition I wish to put forward has to do with the income tax. I think it has a great deal to recommend it, particularly the factor of simplicity. At the present time the government of Canada allows students attending universities and institutions beyond the secondary school level to deduct from their income tax the money they pay out in tuition. This is fine as far as it goes and it certainly has been of assistance to a great many Canadians, particularly people like myself who have found that because of this exemption in one year they were able to continue their education in another year when they were particularly short of funds.
The suggestion which I should like to make is that the government should allow students from areas where there are no universities to deduct from their income tax, or that of their parents, the money that they have to spend for room and board. As an example I should like to refer to myself, when I was attending the University of Manitoba. I lived in a town called Atikokan but I attended the university in Winnipeg. I had to pay room and board, and this was the biggest single expense that I had to bear; the tuition fees were a secondary matter. I understand that nowadays tuition fees have gone up considerably, and now they have become a bigger obstacle for people coming from rural areas and wishing to attend universities in the city.
I suggest that under such a program people rwho live in a city where a university is available should not be exempted, because they have already the option of either staying at home or not. A student coming from an area like mine has no option at all. He must pay room and board if he wishes to attend a university because there are no universities in these areas. Another factor to their disadvantage is that the standard of living in these areas is below that which is in existence in cities. Also the standard of education is not as high, and other facilities such as night schools, correspondence courses or extension courses are not as easily available, if at all. Therefore this is a very important consideration.
In view of the fact that job opportunities for students during the summer months are diminishing as the number of students attending
February 9, 1967

universities increases, students who wish to work their way through college are less often able to do so. In fact for many students this opportunity has disappeared completely.
The second suggestion which I should like to make has to do with federal aid to universities. I recognize, as do most hon. members in the house, that university education is a matter of provincial responsibility. I understand also that the federal government does participate in certain aspects of education, namely in manpower training. However, it does so mainly because of its overriding responsibility for unemployment, and not because it can participate legitimately in education. And yet this happens to come under federal jurisdiction. Nevertheless there are other areas in which the federal government does have responsibility. For example there is the area of the federal government's control over interprovincial truck transportation. Provincial trucking agencies are the responsibility of the provinces, but interprovincial trucking agencies come under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
One of the problems that is facing Canadian universities today is the fact that more students are crossing provincial boundaries to attend university. I am a perfect example of this. I was raised in Ontario and I attended university in Manitoba. It seems to me that just as the federal government has legitimately exerted its jurisdiction in interprovincial trucking, it can also exercise a certain amount of jurisdiction over students who are crossing provincial boundaries to attend universities on the other side. I suggest that the government provide capital funds to universities in which a certain proportion of students come either from outside the country or from other provinces. It should also redeem its promise to provide 10,000 scholarships and to award them to students who attend universities outside their province. It seems to me that this would avoid the constitutional confusion which exists at present, and which prevents the government from assisting in this particular problem. I do not think this would impose a greater burden on the universities and it would provide capital funds for a number of institutions.
I am not suggesting that the government do more than it does at present. As a matter of fact the Department of Indian Affairs and Norther Development does provide capital grants to municipal schools to make available a certain number of places for
The Budget-Mr. Winkler the education of Indians. All I am proposing is something that is in existence already and that is being done in a very successful way. I think that the government might take these two suggestions under consideration as their 1967 centennial project.
May I say to the hon. member who just sat down that I congratulate his father for sending him to university and that I also send him my regrets for the fact that he had to do so.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I thank the Minister of Transport for applauding. I also try to give him as much support as I can.
I regret that the time given me is so short. If I had more time I would have been able to conclude the subject matter before me. However, I am apt to break my train of thought because of the restrictions imposed on me by the shortage of time.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I know that if the minister were in the house he would say that there is another member of the opposition who is trying to tell him how to spend money. The government endeavoured to curtail debate when we were discussing estimates, but in such a debate as this one has an opportunity to advise the government how to spend the funds that are available through taxation.
Tonight, because this is our centennial year and because a certain situation was brought to my attention not too many days ago, I should like to place this matter before the house and the country. This is National Heart Foundation week and I think this matter is an appropriate subject for debate. A few evenings ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) was singing his own praises in regard to the medicare program and the benefits which will flow to Canadians. At one point in his address, when dealing with the question of facilities, and so on, the minister said:
But whether we have medicare or not, we will never have a sufficient supply of personnel and facilities.
This matter was brought to my attention, Mr. Speaker, through a program on the C.B.C. directed by a Mr. Bob Cohen of the press gallery. I found the program very topical and I should like to read an extract from the script in order to put my thoughts on the record:
Canada's medical researchers have just gone through their annual week of meetings.
February 9, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Winkler
These were held at the Chateau Laurier here in Ottawa.
But these seemed to be sessions with a different flavour. Canada's medical scientists are getting more and more anxious about the federal government's lack of support of their research. Last year at this time the government was handed the now-famous Gundy report on medical research in Canada. Charles Gundy is a Toronto financier and chairman of the Hospital for Sick Children. The report said there would be no staff for Canadian medical schools unless the government gave more money for research done by teacher-scientists.
This is the nub of the matter, Mr. Speaker. I believe the teacher-scientist problem is the great one.
Without it, the report suggested, the professional people needed to staff Canada's medical schools would not be attracted to either stay in Canada or come here.
Well, one year later, virtually nothing has happened, The government has expressed sympathy with the researchers' needs. But as one doctor said, "We don't want sympathy, we want firm government policy." Sometimes governments need a bit of a push from outside to establish policy.
I know that this body does not want to become a political pressure group, but I recognize their need. Then the script goes on to point out that the Canadian Association for the Advancement of Health Sciences was established in order to impress upon the government the need in this particular field.
In our centennial year, Mr. Speaker, one of the great things that can be done by Canada is to establish such a program in order to eliminate disease in the world through the means of increased research and scientific development. This would be a lasting monument in this year of celebration that is before us. The government has in many other ways seen fit to spend large sums of money, with which expenditure perhaps I do not disagree. On the other hand, we have commissions and boards spending millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money on projects which are not necessarily what the people of Canada want. They are forced upon the people by the government at a time when a massive, centennial project such as this would be a good and lasting monument throughout the world in this great year of ours.
I shall have to skip a lot of this text, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to bring to the attention of the house and the country one development which has arisen from this meeting of researchers. I should like to draw attention to an invention by a young medical doctor and researcher whom I have known
very slightly during the last few years. The text goes on:
The most exciting research news to come out of the meeting concerns a unique heart operation which promises to be eventually an outstanding procedure for curing the possibly fatal effects of heart attack. It was invented by Dr. Ray Heim-becker, a 43-year-old Toronto surgeon. His research work on the procedure earned him this year's royal college medal in surgery.
This young man, who fortunately had the facilities and the wherewithal to follow up his important work, is making a contribution to Canada and to mankind that cannot be overlooked by the members of this house and by all Canadians. I know that the whole world will benefit from this young man's efforts, and I also know he will also have that satisfaction which comes from hard and earnest endeavour in his chosen profession.
I have before me a letter from the Canadian Heart Foundation which is addressed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and reads as follows:
The provisional committee of the Canadian Association for the Advancement of the Health Sciences is alarmed at the disastrous consequences that would flow from any restraint, even temporary, on the growth of research in Canada. More particularly, we draw your attention to the need to recruit over one thousand teacher-scientists-
Again there is stress upon the teacher-scientist aspect of the profession.
-in the health field to staff our universities in the next five years. Research is essential to the recruitment of this personnel.
We reaffirm the recommendations of the Gundy report as necessary to change the climate of medical research in Canada and urge the government to give an early indication of its long term plans for a drive for medical manpower.
In view of the fact that we are celebrating Heart Foundation Week and that this problem has been with us for some time, I think we should expect some announcement of massive assistance in this as well as in related fields.
Also on the same subject, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read a letter written to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) written by Charles L . Gundy as follows:
The governments in Canada have made it evident that they wish to maintain a first class health care service. It is recognized that to achieve this there must be suitable facilities for medical research and education.
The accompanying report-
Hurry up.

speechtext: May I have that again?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I do not have sufficient time to permit me to say all I should on this matter, but I will do my best.
The accompanying report, "Medical Research in Canada", examines in detail the vital role of medical research in attaining the highest possible standards in the fields of medical education, health care and health services.
The report considers it urgent to establish a favourable medical research environment in Canada which will encourage teacher-scientists-
Once more stress is placed on this teacher-scientist aspect of the question.
-to remain in Canada and in teaching and research, which will attract back to Canadian universities-[DOT]
There has been a tremendous flow of these people out of this country.
-teacher-scientists and graduates now working elsewhere for lack of opportunity in Canada, and which will encourage undergraduates to pursue medical research as a career.
The report states that a failure to establish such an environment in Canada will result in erosion of the standards of Canadian medical schools and the quality of health care provided to the Canadian people.
To establish a favourable medical research environment, the report recommends a major increase in federal government support-
Which is what I am asking for, Mr. Speaker-
-of extramural medical research. Such financial support should be accompanied by a federal government policy statement to assure scientists and potential scientists that there is, and will continue to be, a good future for medical research in this country.
The idea for this report originated in conversations with scientific friends, particularly among the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation and the staff of The Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto. These friends told me of their alarm at the shortage of funds for medical research in Canada and the seriousness of the threat this held for the future of medical standards. Accordingly, Woods, Gordon & Co., management consultants, was commissioned to prepare a study of the problem which led to the report we are now presenting to you.
A list of those endorsing this report is attached-
-and so on.
This report is one of the most comprehensive reports that one could ever read, Mr. Speaker. I contains the material to prove that there is a need and it illustrates what is happening. In this regard I have an editorial in front of me which points out that the $500 million established by the government in the health resources fund is insufficient, that we need a minimum of $100 million a year. The grants the government has been supplying up to the tune of $12 million a year I am sure the house realizes are quite inadequate to meet
The Budget-Mr. Winkler requirements. These amounts are minimal. The stress, as I have said, is upon preparing medical students with ability for the teacher-scientist field.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
This is a priority. The priority should be for medical research and education, as stated by Dr. Merriman, Associate Professor of Medicine in Saskatchewan. When we realize what we spend per capita for this purpose in Canada and compare it with what is being spent in the United States, we realize something lacks in our thinking in this field. They spend in the United States more than 100 per cent more than we spend in Canada-far more. Last year in the United States, from one source alone, the sum raised was $1,072 million. When we realize how much we depend on foreign medical services, on immigrants from other countries, also bearing in mind that we lose as many people to the United States as any other country loses, something should be done. Nothing would be more fitting for our centennial year than a government supported program such as I have talked about. Every member of the house would support it enthusiastically.
I have time to read one short extract from the Gundy report to show the status of research in Canada. Actually, the report covers the entire field. The quotation is as follows:
Research is today an absolutely essential element in the oreparation of young doctors and in the continuing education of established physicians. A medical school can no longer prepare a doctor with the detailed procedures for diagnosis which he will need throughout his later career. The whole art is changing much too fast... medical schools must concentrate on imparting a broad grasp of the basic principles of medicine, and skill in applying these general principles to specific cases. Above all, they must help their students to understand how medical investigation produces new knowledge and how one evaluates the new findings as they appear. This means in turn that most students in good medical schools today must learn the research attitude, even though a majority of them may never become full-fledged research workers themselves.
Brief as that was, lacking in detail as it is, and I wish it had more detail-I am glad that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has just walked in-the extract does permit me to say this. The best centennial project the government of Canada could embark upon would be a massive program in support of research. We need teachers and facilities. I believe that such a program would be the best dedication we could make to our centennial year. It would be to the benefit of all mankind.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELECTRONIC LISTENING DEVICES
CRIMINAL CODE-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELECTRONIC LISTENING DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days ago the Attorney General of the Province of Ontario, Mr. Wishart, made a statement in the Ontario legislature to the effect that Ontario Provincial Police were using wire-tapping equipment for investigation purposes. I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) the following day whether or not the government was giving consideration to the implementation of legislation in this regard. I also asked whether the government would agree to send this whole matter to the standing committee on justice and legal affairs for study. The minister stated that he felt no useful purpose would be served by such referral.
I believe it was Mr. Justice Holmes, that famous United States Supreme Court Justice, who said that wire-tapping is a dirty business. We as Canadians in the past have tended to think if we simply ignore problems, if we do not talk about them and do not admit their existence they will somehow or another go away. Unfortunately it has become obvious in recent years that wire-tapping is taking place in Canada extensively, and police forces as well as private investigation agencies are involved.
A royal commission at the present time is investigating charges of wire-tapping in British Columbia. During the course of the hearings of that commission an R.C.M.P. corporal is reported in the Vancouver Sun of December 7, 1966, as having used this method of investigation. That article in part states:
Richards said he had used listening devices during his 15 years with the R.C.M.P.
He said he had done a two-week course in Ottawa on operating tape recorders with listening devices and was familiar with equipment which does not need wires.
Richards said he has used listening devices in the city of Vancouver on instructions from a higher authority.
An alderman of the city of Saskatoon said that in 1965 he discovered that on the instructions of the chief of police the only telephone available to prisoners in the city jail
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion had been tapped so that police could listen in to phone calls made by prisoners who were awaiting sentence or transfer, or individuals who were in jail but not yet tried. Let me point out that telephone calls of prisoners to their lawyers are highly confidential, and under our law should not be listened to by police.
In 1964 a Toronto Star columnist, Ron Haggart, documented a case of wire-tapping in the city of Toronto. In his column he referred to the name of the officer, the licence number of the R.C.M.P. vehicle used and other pertinent facts.
Bell Telephone officials in the city of Toronto who were interviewed by the Globe and Mail admitted that wire-tapping was taking place, and said it was being done by police officials. It is understood that when it is done by police officials prosecutions were not being pursued.
Members of this house have heard a great deal about the Dorion inquiry. Testimony was given before that inquiry by R.C.M.P. officials that they had wire-tapping equipment and were prepared to use it. Let me quote from page 4815 of the transcript of the Dorion commission. An R.C.M.P. officer, Inspector Carrier, was asked the following question:
Mr. Carrier, do you presently have at your disposal. or did you at that time have, that is to say, did you have at your disposal the necessary technical means to tape, amongst other things, telephone conversations?
The answer was, "Yes." Then at page 4816 Mr. Carrier was asked this question:
Mr. Carrier, does the word "cover", in your mind, simply mean that Mr. Crevier was to sit beside another telephone and listen to the conversation, or could it not also have meant tape the ongoing conversation?
A. It could mean either, either to listen or to record it.
Therefore, it seems to me there is no question that the evidence is conclusive that wiretapping is going on. Newspapers from one end of Canada to the other have written editorials in recent years deploring wire-tapping and calling for legislation to outlaw it. I will not quote them tonight, but I would like to quote a couple of paragraphs from a submission made to the royal commission on civil rights appointed by the Ontario government. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association, an organization in Toronto which includes some
12880	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of the most respected and best known lawyers in the city of Toronto, made a submission to Mr. Justice McRuer. This association said, under the heading, "The Existing Law":
Amazingly enough, there appears to be no legislation of any practical consequence which inhibits scientific invasions of privacy in this jurisdiction. The Criminal Code contains no specific provisions of this nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT RESPECTING ELECTRONIC LISTENING DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of the quotations the hon. member has just put on the record I cannot give any more specific answer than the one I gave the other day, to the effect that I did not think it would be useful to have this matter referred to a parliamentary committee. The reason is that the whole question of wire-tapping is being studied, not only by the department but by a commission of inquiry in British Columbia, and will no doubt also be part of the study made by a commission on crime.
The hon. member referred to wire-tapping as a "dirty business." I would prefer to refer to it as a very difficult problem. I think no one would contradict the stand taken by the hon. member in connection with the protection of civil rights, the independence of individuals and the right to carry on conversations without being overheard. However, I think the hon. member will also realize that an important aspect of our life is the prevention of crime, and national security.
This is one of the problems that government has to resolve. It is a two-edged sword and the question of wire-tapping is not an easy problem to resolve. Wire-tapping is only incidental to a whole series of electronic devices in this area. I feel it is not something with regard to which a decision can be easily or lightly reached.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I believe that the study which will be undertaken in British Columbia will be useful to us. The studies which are now going on in the department as a result of the suggestions made during the meeting of attorneys-general a year ago have also been very useful. However I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North will appreciate fully the difficulties involved and the necessity for coming up with a solution which will in fact bring protection to honest citizens and at the same time permit the government to prevent crime and to

protect our national security. This is what we are trying to do.

maintopic: CANADIAN CENTENNIAL-FAILURE OF ARMED FORCES TATTOO TO APPEAR IN KOOTENAYS
CANADIAN CENTENNIAL-FAILURE OF ARMED FORCES TATTOO TO APPEAR IN KOOTENAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I represent a riding which is very interested in celebrating our centennial year both by public events and by projects that have been carried on, even in some of the quite small communities. Quite recently they heard through the press, on television and on radio, about the proposals for the tattoo train which will be visiting various parts of Canada in the near future. The matter was brought to a head by persons who read the magazine "The Legionary" which is read by about 10,000 people in my riding. I want to quote from this magazine for the minister's information. It reads in part as follows:
The Canadian armed forces will play a large part in Canada's centennial celebrations by taking one of the greatest road shows in Canada's history across the nation.
From St. John's, Newfoundland, to Victoria, British Columbia, Canadians will have the opportunity of seeing the Canadian armed forces tattoo which will be the principal contribution of the services to Canada's centennial celebrations. This colourful spectacle will provide the ultimate in military entertainment within the framework of the development of Canada's armed forces from their French and British origins to our time.
Scheduled to appear at 40 locations across Canada during 1967, the tattoo will feature music, pageantry, colour-sweeping spotlights, history, action, comedy, fantasy and variety to provide entertainment, while at the same time making use of a subtle historical line to link the various scenes.
This was read by a number of people and then the matter was discussed at various meetings of the Legion and of other organizations in my constituency.
I should like to quote a letter which I received from J. C. Hall, president, Pacific Command, Royal Canadian Legion, who happens to be a resident of Trail. It reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
It has been brought to my attention that the Centennial armed forces train which will be travelling across Canada and performing a tattoo at various locations, will not be stopping over in either the East or West Kootenays.
A number of veterans and other citizens have brought this to my attention hoping that the government can be persuaded to have either one or the other section of the trains make a stop in the Kootenays.
As you are aware, the Centennial train itself, is making a short stop of one day in Castlegar, which is considered by the commission to be a central location for some 67,000 residents in this area.
February 9, 1967	COMMONS
This particular location will involve the transportation of thousands of school children a distance over mountain highways of up to 100 miles in order for them to enjoy the Centennial train, which their parents, as taxpayers have contributed to.
In view of the fact, that we have been informed that no change in arrangements for the Centennial trains schedule can be made at this late date,
I hope you can convince the government to take a second look at the schedule for the tattoo train to bring it into the Kootenays.
As a result of that letter and of other correspondence which I received from various persons in Kootenay West I asked the following question in the house on February 6:
I wish to address a question to the Minister of National Defence based on representations from Kootenay West and Kootenay East. Can the minister inform the house why the Canadian armed forces tattoo "Red Train" will not appear in any place in the Kootenays, British Columbia, during centennial year?
At that time, Mr. Speaker, you kindly informed me that this was not the type of question which should be asked at that time. I am therefore taking this opportunity to bring this matter to the attention of the Associate Minister of National Defence and I shall listen with interest to his reply to my plea.

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Associate Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: CANADIAN CENTENNIAL-FAILURE OF ARMED FORCES TATTOO TO APPEAR IN KOOTENAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tattoo itinerary was planned with a great deal of care, bearing in mind that it was intended to take the spectacle to as wide a cross section of the populace as possible. However, from the outset this planning was dominated by a series of rigid criteria, the more significant ones being as follows:
First, the availability of indoor performance facilities from one end of the country to the other at a time of year when arenas were still normally involved with various hockey schedules.
Second, certain anchor dates requiring the tattoo to be in given locations at specified
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion times of year; for example, Expo '67, the C.N.E., and Ottawa as the federal capital.
Third, a mandatory release date for the trains, since the railways required much of the rolling stock used by the tattoo for other purposes before the end of June, 1967.
Fourth, recognition of the fact that, whilst revenue from the tattoo was not necessarily the guiding principle in selecting out of the way performance centres, costs had to be kept continually in mind and responsible judgments reached on the areas in which it would not be economically feasible to appear.
Add to these criteria the fact that there was little more than a six-month period within which to complete the entire project and it will be readily appreciated that there were many deserving areas in which the tattoo could not be presented. The Kootenays happens to be one of these places.
In planning tattoo appearances with the province of British Columbia, Victoria and Vancouver were naturally chosen. Prince George and Kelowna were selected as two additional locations, but only after such factors as time, communications, performance facilities and their availability, geographical situation, and population had been carefully considered. Early in the planning phase these choices were submitted to and approved by the British Columbia centennial committee, which recognized the factors influencing the selection.
The itinerary was therefore approved. It is not considered possible at this time to reexamine the question without jeopardizing the whole program. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the hon. member that this matter will again be referred to the officials, and if I am given any encouragement I will certainly communicate with the hon. member. I will try to do my best to see whether we can accommodate the Kootenays.
